Gaugings of Groupoids, Strings in Shadows, and Emergent Poisson σ \sigma -Models
Rafał R. Suszek

Abstract
. The gauge principle is proposed for rigid Lie-groupoidal symmetries 𝒢 M \hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt of the Polyakov–Alvarez–Gawȩdzki 2 d d non-linear σ \sigma -model with metric target ( M , g M ) (M,{\rm g}_{M}) and the Wess–Zumino term given by a Cheeger–Simons differential character coming from an abelian gerbe 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . The principle bases on the notion of principaloid bundle with connection ( 𝒫 , Θ ) (\mathscr{P},\Theta) , introduced by Strobl and the Author. The descent of the model to the shadow of 𝒫 \mathscr{P} is demonstrated to require a twisted 𝒢 \mathscr{G} -equivariant structure on 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , prequantising a multiplicative extension ( H M , ρ , 0 ) (H_{M},\rho,0) of the gerbe’s curvature H M H_{M} to a 3-cocycle in the Bott–Schulman–Stasheff cohomology of the groupoid’s nerve. The descent is accompanied by a combined g M {\rm g}_{M} -isometric/ ρ \rho -holonomic reduction of the structure group of 𝒫 \mathscr{P} , and uses an augmentation of the original gerbe by a trivial one depending quadratically on Θ \Theta . The latter couples to the field of the σ \sigma -model—in an extension of the scheme worked out for the action groupoid by Gawȩdzki, Waldorf and the Author—through the comomentum component of the Spencer pair of ρ \rho , as described by Crainic et al . A fully fledged cohomological analysis of the relevant gauge anomaly and of inequivalent gaugings is presented. In the symplectic setting, the augmentation procedure is shown to lead to the emergence of the standard Poisson σ \sigma -model. Conversely, a coaugmentation of a (local) Poisson σ \sigma -model by a flat equivariant gerbe yields a novel field theory with the shadow of the underlying symplectic principaloid bundle as the configuration bundle, and with manifest lagrangean gauge symmetry. A simple Cartan-type associating mechanism is proposed to account for the reduction of the structure group of the principaloid bundle. The mechanism allows for the coupling of an arbitrary number of distinct charged matter-field species to a given gauge field.



Dedicated to Thomas Strobl, a dear Friend,

on the happy occasion of His 60(+1). birthday.

1.
Introduction

The concept of gauge symmetry and the construct of gauge field theory have long enjoyed the status of constitutive elements of modern physical thinking and modelling. On one hand, they serve to explain deviations of classical trajectories of charged probes—such as those observed in the Wilson cloud chamber—and interference patterns for their Feynman histories—such as those measured in the Aharonov–Bohm experiment—from those of neutral objects propagating in a given spacetime in the presence of external gauge fields. In this case, the coupling between the gauge field and the probe resp. the said interference are typically represented by a suitable transport operator resp. the corresponding differential character (holonomy) on Ehresmann’s bundle of gauges with compatible connection, which geometrises the gauge field
[
Alv85
,
Gaw88
]
. The last 40 years have seen tremendous progress in the study of gauge theory thus understood for arbitrary
p
-form gauge fields in terms of higher homological algebra and category theory, see:
[
BJFJ+25
]
for a recent review. On the other hand, the two—the concept and the construct—provide us with a coherent framework in which to formulate dynamics of fields with configuration spaces modelled on orbispaces—singular in general—for various symmetry models,
e.g.
, orbifolds, quotients of Lie-group actions, orientifolds
etc.

[
GR03
,
GSW08
,
GSW11a
,
GSW10
,
GSW13
]
. Here, it is the gaug
ing
of a rigid symmetry of a given field theory, and the resulting gauge field-mediated—
e.g.
, through the minimal coupling—descent of dynamics to Cartan’s associated bundles over the spacetime of arbitrary topology that play a key rôle, and equivariant cohomology becomes an indispensable tool. Also in this model-building context, there has recently been much progress—the systematic gerbe-theoretic construction and cohomological classification of the Gawȩdzki–Kupiainen coset
\sigma
-models of the 2
d
RCFT, worked out by Gawȩdzki
et al.

[
GSW10
,
GSW13
,
dFGT14
]
, is an important example. We make the latter aspect of gauge theory the general theme of the present work.

The classic formulation of gauge theory, referred to above, bases on a particular choice of the symmetry model, which by now has become essentially synonymous with the notion of symmetry, to wit: a group
{\rm G}
acting on the configuration fibre
M
of the field theory as
\lambda\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\to{\rm Diff}(M)
. The inherent rigidity of this model and the ensuing limitations of its applicability in realistic configurational geometries were demonstrated convincingly by Weinstein
[
Wei96
]
: Given a group
{\rm G}
acting on a manifold
M
by automorphisms of the structure present on
M
(
e.g.
, by diffeomorphisms in the generic situation), the removal of
some but not all
points from some of the
{\rm G}
-orbits—which clearly does
not
affect the
local
geometric equivalences, away from the excisions—leads to the disappearance of
{\rm G}
as a
global
symmetry model. Recovering the local symmetry within the smooth paradigm calls for a renewed conceptualisation of the notion of symmetry, which allows for a fibration of the symmetry model over the space whose symmetries we seek to describe, but now nontrivial and without a typical fibre in general. Thus, we arrive at a
specialised
internalisation in the smooth category
{\rm{\bf Man}}
of the concept of equivalence relation between points in
M
, forming a set
\mathscr{G}
:

\bullet

reflexivity
: identity maps are among (self-)equivalences,

\bullet

smoothness
:
\mathscr{G}
carries a smooth structure,
and
equivalences ‘chart’
M
in that for every equivalence
g\in\mathscr{G}
there is a submanifold
O_{g}\ni g
in
\mathscr{G}
such that
t(O_{g})\cong O_{g}\cong s(O_{g})
(diffeomorphisms).

Altogether, these elementary requirements determine a
Lie groupoid

The construction at the core of the classic gauge theory for symmetries with a Lie-group model is Ehresmann’s principal bundle of gauges

The choice of the corresponding generalisation for symmetries modelled on arbitrary Lie groupoids calls for some caution, lest the principle of homogeneity of internal structures of the field theory—such as the reference frames, or internal degrees of freedom—should be violated, which we choose to avoid. N_{\bullet}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
. Such extensions have been shown to canonically induce vertical vector-bundle morphisms
\kappa\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{E}\to{\rm T}^{*}M
—dubbed (2-)
comomenta
in the present context—as part of Spencer data of
\rho
, discovered by Crainic
et al.
in
[
CS15
]
. An immediate consequence of the assumption is the reduction of the structure group of
\mathscr{P}
to the
\rho
-holonomic group

{\mathbb{B}}_{\rho}(\mathscr{G})=\{\ \beta\in{\rm Bisec}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)\ |\ \beta^{*}\rho=0\ \}
, suggested by the aforementioned bi-module/symmetry correspondence. Crucially, the comomentum has been proven equivariant with respect to canonical actions of
{\mathbb{B}}_{\rho}(\mathscr{G})
on its domain and codomain. Whenever there exists a bicategorial geometrisation of the BSS 3-cocycle
(H_{M},\rho,0)
in the form of a
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure on

\mathcal{G}
, the reduction is readily seen to ensure effective descent—in the sense of Breen’s 2-stack structure on the smooth site
{\rm{\bf Man}}
, realised by gerbes
[
Ste00
]
—of a gerbe over
\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{-1}\mathcal{O}
obtained from
\mathcal{G}
through its augmentation by (the pullback of) a trivial gerbe on
\bigsqcup_{i\in I}\,O_{i}\times M
determined by the comomentum
\kappa
coupled to the local gauge field in a way essentially dictated by the pioneering analysis of
[
GSW10
]
. The descended gerbe over
\mathscr{F}
has been verified to define a
gauge-invariant
holonomy (Thm.
8.6
).

The existence of a twisted equivariant structure on a gerbe may, in general, be obstructed topologically, which—as argued extensively in
[
GSW10
]
in the case of group-modelled symmetry—leads to various pathologies upon quantisation of the PAG
\sigma
-model coupled to the gauge field in the manner described above. Hence, it is vital to identify and quantify the obstructions, also known as
gauge anomalies
. This goal has been attained in the case under consideration in terms of a
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant—
i.e.
, simplicial, over
N_{\bullet}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
—extension of the standard Beilinson–Deligne hypercohomology describing 0-, 1- and 2-cells of the bicategory of gerbes over a given base. The same formalism has been employed to classify inequivalent gaugings, represented by non-cohomologous
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structures on a given target gerbe. Both results—the anomaly analysis (Props.
9.3
,
9.5
and
9.7
) and the classification (Prop.

)—extend straightforwardly (and are motivated by) those derived in
[
GSW10
]
.

Whenever a multiplicative extension
\rho
exists, and the gauge anomaly vanishes, a
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure on the target gerbe from any one of the equivalence classes identified above can be used to define a
gauged PAG
\sigma
-model
with the configuration bundle given by a shadow
\mathscr{F}
of an arbitrary principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle with the structure group fully reduced as
{\rm Bisec}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)\searrow t_{*}^{-1}({\rm Isom}(M,{\rm g}_{M}))\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\rho}(\mathscr{G})\equiv{\mathbb{B}}_{\sigma}(\mathscr{G})
(Thm.
10.1
). The latter group can be viewed as composed by a family of distinguished submanifolds within the arrow manifold
\mathscr{G}
which project diffeomorphically onto
M
along both: the source map and the target map. In this picture, the structure group of the principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}
prior to the background-enforced reduction,
{\rm Bisec}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
, yields—for a class of Lie groupoids, and among them those canonically associated with integrable Lie algebroids (as well as arbitrary group-action groupoids)—the most complete realisation of the structure groupoid within

that can be conceived, namely one with an element
\beta\in{\rm Bisec}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
through

.

There is an important theoretical context in which the hitherto general considerations concretise and gain even more structure, to wit—the geometry of Weinstein’s symplectic groupoids
[
Wei87
,
CDW87
]
, with its deep conceptual relation to Kontsevich’s (deformation) quantisation
[
Kon03
]
, mediated by (topological) field theory in the manner originally uncovered by Cattaneo and Felder
[
CF00a
,
CF00b
]
. An attempt—made in Sec.
11
—at internalising the former results in the symplectic category leads to an unexpected finding: Given a symplectic groupoid
(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\omega)
, with its multiplicative symplectic 2-form
\omega\in Z^{2}(\mathscr{G})
and its canonically Poisson object manifold
(M,\Pi)
, the holonomy of the previously mentioned (trivial-gerbe) augmentation of a gerbe
\mathcal{G}
over
M
endowed with an
\omega
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure reproduces—upon specialisation to the trivial symplectic principaloid bundle, with the structure group reduced to the subgroup
{\mathbb{B}}_{\omega}(\mathscr{G})
of
lagrangean bisections
—the DF amplitude of the Poisson
\sigma
-model on the cotangent algebroid over
(M,\Pi)

[
Ike94
,
SS94
]
. This provides us with an intricate, novel conceptualisation of the Poisson
\sigma
-model—as a flat trivial twist of the gerbe of a (dynamical) PAG
\sigma
-model on the Poisson target
(M,\Pi)
, untwisting that gerbe’s
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure—and leads, through the reversal of the logic of the original gauging procedure, to an extension of the hitherto definition of the Poisson
\sigma
-model which promotes the latter to the rank of a (topological) field theory with a Lie-groupoidal gauge symmetry modelled on the group
t_{*}({\mathbb{B}}_{\omega}(\mathscr{G}))
of Poisson diffeomorphisms. The extension consists in co-augmenting the said trivial gerbe with an arbitrary
\omega
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant gerbe over
M
. By previous results, such a co-augmentation automatically allows to extend—through the (2-)stacky descent—the definition of the field theory further to Poisson shadow bundles of
arbitrary
topology (Thm.
11.4
). In the light of the previous remarks, this permits us to think of the novel field theory as one with the effective configuration fibre
M//\mathscr{G}
. Given the structural interpretation of the Euler–Lagrange equations of the Poisson
\sigma
-model as defining Lie-algebroid morphisms
[
BKS05
]
, special attention has been given to the distinguished co-augmentations which leave these equations unchanged—the
flat coaugmentations
, characterised in natural cohomological terms in Prop.
11.6
.

The present work presents the first physical application of the abstract mathematical constructs introduced in the precursor paper
[
SS25
]
. Bearing in mind its character, we have gone to great lengths (
sic
!) to make it self-contained, and thus more easily accessible—this is the rationale behind the many examples scattered in the main text, and the numerous appendices. Understandably, the work leaves a number of questions open, and prompts further research in several directions—both have been addressed in the concluding Sec.
12
. We hope to return to them in a future study.

2.
A groupoidal reformulation of the classic gauge principle

The main goal of the present investigation is the formulation of a gauge principle for rigid configurational symmetries of a dynamical system modelled on a Lie groupoid, and its subsequent application in a field-theoretic setting of choice. The path towards the goal thus set is bound to lead through and, in so doing, subsume the classic gauge principle for Lie group-modelled symmetries, whose geometric foundations were laid by Ehresmann
[
Ehr50
]
and Cartan
[
Car50
]
. A careful reformulation of this prototypical construction in the language of the theory of Lie groupoids and their tangent algebroids affords us the opportunity to identify the key components of the classic principle and structural relations between them, which we may subsequently employ as the basis of the desired generalisation. This is, then, the course of action that we take below. (As the raw mathematical content of the present discussion, as well as its physical interpretation are completely standard by now, we choose a narrative, descriptive mode of exposition instead of the formal, definition-theorem-proof one, which we reserve for the remainder of the paper.)

Ehresmann’s classic construction begins from a choice of a manifold
M
modelling the space of internal degrees of freedom of the field theory-to-be over a given spacetime
\Sigma
, accompanied by a choice of a Lie group
{\rm G}
of symmetries
\lambda\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\to{\rm Diff}(M)
of the field’s dynamics. The latter are interpreted passively as distinguished redefinitions of an internal reference frame (or
gauge
). There then follows an identification of a smooth homogeneous distribution, over
\Sigma
, of “observers” (as they are expressly called by Pradines in
[
Pra07
]
), each of which is represented by a
{\rm G}
-torsor of equivalent choices of an internal reference frame for his or her observations/measurements of a physical (matter) field. The ensuing trivial local models
O_{i}\times{\rm G}
of the distribution of frames over an open cover
\mathcal{O}\equiv\{O_{i}\}_{i\in I}
of
\Sigma
are glued together over non-empty intersections
O_{ij}\equiv O_{i}\cap O_{j}
by smoothly
O_{ij}
-indexed families of diffeomorphisms of the typical fibre
{\rm G}
which commute with the right regular action
r\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\times{\rm G}\to{\rm G},\ (g,h)\mapsto g\cdot h
of the structure groupoid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}\equiv\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{{\rm G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\bullet}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
(see: Ex.
B.2
) on
{\rm G}
. The latter action represents a global (vertical) choice of frame. This yields a principal
{\rm G}
-bundle of gauges over
\Sigma
:

(2.1)

G})/\sim_{l_{g_{\cdot\cdot}}}\,,\qquad(\sigma,j,g)\sim\bigl(\sigma,i,g_{ij}(\sigma)\cdot g\bigr)\,,

with a (principal fibrewise right) action
r_{P}
of
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
on its total space
P
, modelled—through
{\rm G}
-equivariant local trivialisations
P\tau_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:\pi_{P}^{-1}(O_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}O_{i}\times{\rm G}
—on the aforementioned right regular action
r
on the typical fibre
{\rm G}
, and with the gluing realised in terms of the left regular action
l\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\to{\rm Diff}({\rm G}),\ h\mapsto h\cdot(\cdot)\equiv l_{h}(\cdot)
of the transition 1-cocycle
g_{ij}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{ij}\to{\rm G}
.

Next, we use the principle of
r_{P}({\rm G})
-equivariance to distinguish those bundle automorphisms of
P
which—similarly to the local gluings—commute with global redefinitions of frame,

\displaystyle{\rm Aut}(P)={\rm Aut}_{{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)}(P)\cap{\rm Diff}_{r_{P}({\rm G})}(P)\,.

In the local (trivialised) picture, these are represented by smooth maps from the base
\Sigma
into
{\rm G}
realised on the typical fibre by
l
, as before. As understood by Ehresmann already in
[
Ehr50
]
, their action on
P
admits a straightforward Lie-groupoidal description: The distinguished automorphisms are in bijection with global bisections of the Ehresmann–Atiyah (or gauge) groupoid
(P\times P)/{\rm G}\equiv{\rm At}(P)
(see: Def.
B.7
). The groupoid acts on
P
along
\Sigma
from the left as
\lambda_{P}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm At}(P)\times_{\Sigma}P\to P,\ ([(p_{2},p_{1})],p_{1})\mapsto p_{2}
, with moment map given by the base projection
\pi_{\Sigma}
(see: Def.
B.20
). The restriction of the action to any one of the bisections reproduces the corresponding automorphism. The action commutes with the right defining action
r_{P}
of the structure groupoid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
, and the latter preserves the moment map
\pi_{\Sigma}
by definition. Moreover,
\lambda_{P}
is manifestly principal relative to the canonical map
P\dashedrightarrow\bullet
to the object manifold of the structure groupoid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
, so that a prototypical bi-bundle arises in the sense of Def.
B.30
:

Inspection of the anatomy of the gauge groupoid reveals additional structure behind the above picture:
{\rm At}(P)
is a fibre-bundle object in the category of Lie groupoids, with base
{\rm Pair}(\Sigma)
and typical fibre
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
. Its action
\lambda_{P}
on
P
covers the canonical left-fibred action of its base on that of
P
(see: Ex.
B.22
), and is locally modelled on the canonical left-fibred action of its fibre on that of
P
. Thus, altogether, we discover the (left) trident (see: Def.
B.32
)

\displaystyle P\tau_{i}\circ\chi\circ P\tau_{i}^{-1}(\sigma,g)=\bigl(\sigma,h_{i}(\sigma)\cdot g\bigr)

as

The next stage of the classic construction, worked out by Cartan

Car50
]
(see also:

]

{\rm G}

\Sigma
, with typical fibre given by the arrow manifold
{\rm G}\times M
of the action groupoid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
associated with the smooth action
\lambda
(see: Ex.
B.5
). The groupoid acts (fibrewise from the right) on the total space of the extended bundle in a manner which emulates the diagonal action of
{\rm G}
combining
r_{P}
an
\lambda
,
i.e.
, through

(2.3)

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\widetilde{\lambda}\hskip-2.0pt:(P\times M)\times_{M}({\rm G}\times M)\longrightarrow P\times M,\ \bigl((p,m),\bigl(g,\lambda_{g^{-1}}(m)\bigr)\bigr)\longmapsto\bigl(r_{P}(p,g),\lambda_{g^{-1}}(m)\bigr)\,.

The action being free and proper, there emerges a smooth quotient manifold
(P\times M)/{\rm G}\equiv(P\times M)/({\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M)\equiv P\times_{\lambda}M
, which fibres over
\Sigma

of the previously identified structure groupoid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M

is modelled on the target map
\lambda
between the respective typical fibres, and so we arrive at a non-trivial principal
{\rm G}{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
-bundle
P\times M\to P\times_{\lambda}M
in the slice over
\Sigma

The quotient
\pi_{\sim}
realises an important conceptual objective: It couples the choice of a reference frame to the outcome of an ‘observation’ of a (local) physical field
\varphi\hskip-2.0pt:O\to M
(over
O\subset\Sigma
) through the identity

\displaystyle[(r_{P}(p,g),\varphi(\sigma))]\equiv[(p,\lambda_{g}(\varphi(\sigma)))]\,.

Thus, ‘observations’ of a matter field
\varphi\in\Gamma(P\times_{\lambda}M)
, carried out in local trivialisations
\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:\pi_{P\times_{\lambda}M}^{-1}(O_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}O_{i}\times M,\ i\in I
and represented by smooth maps
\varphi_{i}={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\varphi\big|_{O_{i}}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\to M
, are related over intersections
O_{ij}\ni\sigma
of the respective domains by the transition 1-cocycle of
P
as

\displaystyle\varphi_{i}(\sigma)=\lambda_{g_{ij}(\sigma)}\bigl(\varphi_{j}(\sigma)\bigr)\,.

In fact, the latter structure is far from generic due to the cartesian factorisation of the total space of the fibre bundle
P\times M\to\Sigma
, implying, in particular, that the gluing of the bundle’s local trivialisations is realised by the transition 1-cocycle of the sub-structure
P\to\Sigma
, taking values in
{\rm G}
. This conforms with the identification of
{\rm G}
as the symmetry/equivalence structure, which relates local descriptions (trivialisations) of the field bundle
P\times_{\lambda}M
. Hence, effectively, the structure groupoid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
(whose action is emulated by that of
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
) and the structure group of the extended bundle
P\times M
coincide—we see the Lie group
{\rm G}
in both rôles. The resultant erasure of ontological/functional distinction between the two entities in the prototypical construction obscures the path to generalisation. Restoring the two functional types was the first step on that path undertaken in
[
SS25
]
, which we recapitulate in the next section.

The non-genericity noted above propagates to the next level, on which distinguished automorphisms of the associated bundle
P\times_{\lambda}M
are induced from those of the extended bundle
P\times M
. The former being recognised as a configuration bundle of a field theory with the
group
symmetry
{\rm G}
gauged, we are naturally interested in automorphisms with a local model furnished by the symmetry equivalence
\lambda
. These are induced—by the very construction of the principal bundle
P\times M\to P\times_{\lambda}M
—from
{\rm G}
-equivariant automorphisms of
P
previously encoded in the construction of the Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid of the bundle of gauges
P
. In particular, the vertical ones
\mathscr{F}_{*}(\chi)\in{\rm Aut}_{{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)/\Sigma}(P\times_{\lambda}M)
among them—termed gauge transformations—are locally presented as

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\mathscr{F}_{*}(\chi)\circ\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}^{-1}(\sigma,m)=\bigl(\sigma,\lambda_{h_{i}(\sigma)}(m)\bigr)\,,

with the
h_{i}
as before. Thus, we arrive at—non-generic from the point of view of the structure of the action groupoid—
extended
trident of the Cartan construction:

whose left wing, with its lifted action

\displaystyle\widetilde{\lambda}{}_{P}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm At}(P)\times_{\Sigma}(P\times M)\longrightarrow P\times M,\ \bigl([(p_{2},p_{1})],(p_{1},m)\bigr)\longmapsto(p_{2},m)

descending to the quotient as

\displaystyle\lambda_{P\times_{\lambda}M}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm At}(P)\times_{\Sigma}(P\times_{\lambda}M)\longrightarrow P\times_{\lambda}M,\ \bigl([(p_{2},p_{1})],[(p_{1},m)]\bigr)\longmapsto[(p_{2},m)]

(due to the mutual commutativity of
\widetilde{\lambda}{}_{P}
and
\widetilde{\lambda}
), captures the automorphisms of interest through restriction of the latter action to bisections within the arrow manifold
{\rm At}(P)
of the gauge groupoid.

The Ehresmann–Cartan construction rephrased above readily lifts to the tangents of the three bundles:
P,P\times M
, and
P\times_{\lambda}M
, giving rise to distinguished Ehresmann connections, with the respective horizontal distributions: a
{\rm G}
-invariant one

over

à la Kobayashi–Nomizu
[

{\rm G}

through the verticalised derivative

\displaystyle\nabla^{\mathcal{A}}\hskip-2.0pt:\Gamma(P\times_{\lambda}M)\ni\varphi\longmapsto\Theta_{P\times_{\lambda}M}\circ{\rm T}\varphi\equiv\nabla^{\mathcal{A}}\varphi\in\Gamma\bigl({\rm T}^{*}\Sigma\otimes\varphi^{*}{\rm V}(P\times_{\lambda}M)\bigr)\,,

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}\equiv{\rm T}\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\nabla^{\mathcal{A}}\varphi={\rm T}\varphi_{i}-\mathcal{K}^{M}(\varphi_{i})\circ A_{i}\,.

These local objects exhibit simple (tensorial) behaviour:

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A^{\chi}_{i}}\bigl(\chi\circ\varphi\bigr)_{i}(\sigma)={\rm T}_{\varphi_{i}(\sigma)}\lambda_{h_{i}(\sigma)}\circ\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}\,,\qquad\sigma\in O_{i}

under a
simultaneous
gauge transformation of the (local) matter field:

\displaystyle\varphi_{i}(\cdot)\longmapsto\lambda_{h_{i}(\cdot)}\bigl(\varphi_{i}(\cdot)\bigr)\equiv(\mathscr{F}_{*}(\chi)\circ\varphi)_{i}(\cdot)\,,

and that of the (local) gauge field:

(2.8)

\displaystyle A_{i}\longmapsto{\rm T}_{e}{\rm Ad}_{h_{i}}\circ A_{i}+h_{i}^{*}\theta_{\rm R}\equiv A^{\chi}_{i}\,.

The form of the latter is a consequence of having promoted
\chi
to the rank of a connection-preserving automorphism of
P
, with

(2.9)

\displaystyle\chi^{*}\mathcal{A}^{\chi}\equiv\mathcal{A}^{\chi}\circ{\rm T}\chi=\mathcal{A}\,.

Accordingly, given a

The assumed

\displaystyle\underline{\mathcal{T}[\mathcal{A}]}\in\Gamma({\rm T}^{*}(P\times_{\lambda}M)^{\otimes n})

with the property

\displaystyle\check{\pi}_{P\times_{\lambda}M}^{*}\underline{\mathcal{T}[\mathcal{A}]}=\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}[\mathcal{A}]\,.

This is a simple manifestation of the sheaf property of
\Gamma({\rm T}^{*}(P\times_{\lambda}M)^{\otimes n})
. The descended tensor

can now be used in the definition of a coupling

\displaystyle\left\langle\underline{\mathcal{T}[\mathcal{A}]},{\rm T}\varphi^{\otimes n}\right\rangle

6
, alongside an important illustration of a more general gauging scheme relevant in the presence of non-tensorial topological couplings.

We close this section with an answer to the natural question about the geometric significance of the choice of (the isoclass of) the bundle of gauges underlying the construction reviewed above. The answer reveals the actual meaning of the latter, and—in so doing—emphasises its usefulness as one of systematic procedures that serve to chart the universe of field theories. 3.
Principaloid bundles with connection and their Godement quotients

In this section, we recapitulate the essential elements of the recent proposal—due to Strobl and the Author
[
SS25
]
—of a mathematical construction underlying the gauge principle for a symmetry modelled on an arbitrary Lie groupoid, based on
the fundamental assumption of homogeneity of the distribution of internal structures
(field degrees of freedom, gauges,
etc.
)
over the spacetime of the physical model
. The construction generalises, in a nontrivial manner, the one from the previous section, employed in the gauging of symmetries with the (Lie-)group model. (Proofs of propositions and theorems quoted in this section can be found in
[
SS25
]
.)

3.1.
The bundles

We begin with a generalisation of Ehresmann’s concept of bundle of gauges, or reference frames under equivalence
6
6

6

These were also referred to by Pradines
[
Pra07
]
as ‘measures of events’, or ‘observations’, carried out by ‘observers’ (represented by fibres of the bundle).
. We model the totality of these frames by the arrow manifold of a given Lie groupoid, which is then promoted to the rank of the typical fibre of the resultant fibre bundle, in keeping with the assumption of homogeneity. Furthermore, we take as the organising principle of our subsequent construction equivariance with respect to the canonical right-fibred action of the Lie groupoid on the latter manifold, admitting a smooth quotient.

Corollary 3.2
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.19
. A principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}\to\Sigma
from Def.

admits a model

(3.1)

\displaystyle\mathscr{P}\cong\bigsqcup_{i\in I}\,(O_{i}\times\mathscr{G})/\sim_{L_{\beta_{\cdot\cdot}}}\,,\qquad\qquad(\sigma_{2},j,g_{2})\sim(\sigma_{1},i,g_{1})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\sigma_{1},g_{1})=\bigl(\sigma_{2},L_{\beta_{ij}(\sigma_{1})}(g_{2})\bigr)\,,

(3.2)

relative to the open cover
\mathcal{O}
, and for a
transition 1-cocycle

\displaystyle\beta_{ij}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{ij}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\,,

satisfying the

(3.3)

\displaystyle\beta_{ij}\cdot\beta_{jk}\big|_{O_{ijk}}=\beta_{ik}\big|_{O_{ijk}}\,,

and realised by the left-multiplication

It is worth noting that the
realisation

\{L_{\beta_{ij}}\}_{i,j\in I}
carries exactly the same (sheaf-theoretic) information as the underlying 1-cocycle
\{\beta_{ij}\}_{i,j\in I}

. In this manner, the finite-dimensional principaloid bundle becomes
uniquely
associated with the generically infinite-dimensional principal
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
-bundle over its base, represented by the transition 1-cocycle.

The special character of the action of the structure groupoid on the total space of the principaloid bundle leads to the emergence of a daughter fibre bundle over the same base as a smooth quotient relative to that action.

By its very construction, generalising that of the classic group quotient

, the new bundle becomes a natural candidate for the configuration bundle of a gauge(d) field theory-to-be. Its global sections
\varphi\in\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
, to be interpreted as (charged-matter) fields of the said theory, admit—through local trivialisations
\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{-1}(O_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}O_{i}\times M
—the anticipated presentation by locally smooth maps
\varphi_{i}:={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\varphi\big|_{O_{i}}
to the space
M
of internal degrees of freedom of the theory, related by local gauge (or reference-frame) redefinitions
t_{*}(\beta_{ij}(\sigma))
over intersections
O_{ij}\ni\sigma
of their respective domains.

The fundamental feature of the bundle object (
3.21
) is the existence of a coherent lift of the canonical action of its base
{\rm Pair}(\Sigma)
on that of the principaloid bundle to the respective total spaces. The lift commutes with
\varrho
, and so it descends to the shadow. This is crucial for the induction of distinguished automorphisms of the latter bundle from the
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant ones of the principaloid bundle, as shall be recalled in the next (sub)section.

Theorem 3.8
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.7
and
B.32
. The Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})
acts on the principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
and its shadow
\mathscr{F}
in the following way:

\bullet

On every principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
, there exists a canonical structure of a left
{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})
-module, with momentum
\mu_{\mathscr{P}}=\mathscr{D}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{P}\to\mathscr{F}
and action

(3.23)

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\lambda_{\mathscr{P}}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm At}(\mathscr{P}){}_{{\mathsf{S}}}\hskip-2.0pt\times_{\mathscr{D}}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{P}\longrightarrow\mathscr{P},\ \bigl([(\sigma_{1},g,\sigma_{2},i,j)],[(\sigma_{2},h,k)]\bigr)\longmapsto[(\sigma_{1},g.(\beta_{jk}(\sigma_{2})\vartriangleright h),i)]\,,

written in the local models: (
3.9
) for
{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})
and (
3.2
) for
\mathscr{P}
, for
\sigma_{1}\in O_{i}
and
\sigma_{2}\in O_{jk}
.

\bullet

This structure covers the canonical structure of a left
{\rm Pair}(\Sigma)
-module on
\Sigma
, with momentum
\mu_{\Sigma}\equiv{\rm id}_{\Sigma}
and action

\displaystyle\lambda_{\Sigma}\hskip-2.0pt:(\Sigma\times\Sigma)\,{}_{{\rm pr}_{2}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{{\rm id}_{\Sigma}}\hskip-2.0pt\Sigma\longrightarrow\Sigma,\ \bigl((\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}),\sigma_{2}\bigr)\longmapsto\sigma_{1}\,.

\bullet

On the corresponding shadow
\mathscr{F}
, there exists a canonical structure of a left
{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})
-module, with momentum
\mu_{\mathscr{F}}={\rm id}_{\mathscr{F}}
and action

(3.24)

\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathscr{F}}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm At}(\mathscr{P}){}_{{\mathsf{S}}}\hskip-2.0pt\times_{{\rm id}_{\mathscr{F}}}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{F}\longrightarrow\mathscr{F},\ \bigl([(\sigma_{1},g,\sigma_{2},i,j)],[(\sigma_{2},m,k)]\bigr)\longmapsto[(\sigma_{1},t(g),i)]\,.

\bullet

The action
\lambda_{\mathscr{P}}
is intertwined with
\lambda_{\mathscr{F}}
by the sitting-duck map
\mathscr{D}
, as reflected in the identities

(3.25)

\displaystyle\mu_{\mathscr{P}}=\mu_{\mathscr{F}}\circ\mathscr{D}\,,\qquad\qquad\lambda_{\mathscr{F}}\circ\bigl({\rm id}_{{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})}\times\mathscr{D}\bigr)=\mathscr{D}\circ\lambda_{\mathscr{P}}\,.

In particular, there exists a division map

(3.27)

\displaystyle\psi_{\mathscr{P}}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{P}\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\mu}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{P}\longrightarrow{\rm At}(\mathscr{P})

with the property

(3.28)

\displaystyle(\psi_{\mathscr{P}},{\rm pr}_{2})=(\lambda_{\mathscr{P}},{\rm pr}_{2})^{-1}\,.

The above construction is readily seen to subsume the classic ones, long-known to capture the geometry of the gauge principle for group-modelled symmetries.

as its shadow. As for every principaloid bundle, there exists an Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(P\times M)
, which, however, has not been considered in the classic setting. The obvious reason for that is the existence of the abstract symmetry model
{\rm G}
, which subsequently enters the definition of the gauge group, whence the more complex structure of the extended trident (
2.5
). The symmetry model
{\rm G}
is typically distinguished as a finite-dimensional subgroup within the group of diffeomorphisms of the configuration fibre
M
of a given field theory consisting of those diffeomorphisms which preserve some additional geometric structure on
M
determining the dynamics of that field theory, such as, e.g., a metric tensor, or a Maxwell field etc. As we shall see in Sec.
7
(and as has long been known, e.g., in the symplectic/Poisson setting of
[
Wei87
,
CDW87
]
, see:
[
Ryb01
]
), putting such extra structure on the object (resp. arrow) manifold of a given Lie groupoid also leads, in general, to a reduction of the group of bisections to a subgroup composed of those bisections which preserve the extra structure when realised through
t_{*}
(resp.
L
) as diffeomorphisms of
M
(resp.
\mathscr{G}
). Anticipating this eventuality, we shall consider the groupoidal variant of Cartan’s associating construction in Sec.
4
.

3.2.
The automorphisms, and gauge transformations

The principle of
\mathscr{G}
-equivariance, introduced in the previous section, leads directly to an adaptation of the notion of automorphism.

Definition 3.11
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.1
. We call a bundle automorphism of a principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}

\mathscr{G}
-principal
, or simply an
automorphisms of
\mathscr{P}
, if it is
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant. Whenever, in addition, it covers the identity on the base
\Sigma
, we term it
vertical
, or a
gauge transformation
. The
group of

automorphisms
of
\mathscr{P}
shall be denoted as

\displaystyle{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})\equiv{\rm Aut}_{{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)}(\mathscr{P})\cap{\rm Diff}_{\varrho(\mathscr{G})}(\mathscr{P})\,,

and its subgroup composed of vertical automorphisms, to be referred to as the
gauge group
of
\mathscr{P}
, as

\displaystyle{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})\equiv{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})_{\rm vert}\,.

Upon invoking Prop.
B.23
once more, we establish

Corollary 3.12
.

Adopt the notation of Cor.
3.2
and Def.
3.11
. A gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
admits a local presentation by smooth maps valued in the structure group
L({\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G}))
of
\mathscr{P}
, i.e.,

\displaystyle\Phi\big|\hskip-2.0pt:\pi_{\mathscr{P}}^{-1}(O_{i})\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_{\mathscr{P}}^{-1}(O_{i}),\ \mathscr{P}\tau_{i}^{-1}(\sigma,g)\longmapsto\mathscr{P}\tau_{i}^{-1}\bigl(\sigma,L_{\gamma_{i}(\sigma)}(g)\bigr)

for some family of smooth maps

\displaystyle\gamma_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\,,\quad i\in I\,,

satisfying the
gauge 1-coboundary identities

(3.29)

\displaystyle\beta_{ij}\cdot\gamma_{j}\big|_{O_{ij}}=\gamma_{i}\cdot\beta_{ij}\big|_{O_{ij}}\,.

The equivariance of the automorphisms of the principaloid bundle distinguished above enables us to push them down to the shadow along the quotient map
\mathscr{D}
.

Proposition 3.13
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.11
and Thm.
3.3
. There is a canonical group homomorphism

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{*}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})\longrightarrow{\rm Aut}_{{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)}(\mathscr{F})\,,

which induces an action of
{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})
on
\mathscr{F}
intertwined by the sitting-duck map, as determined by the identity

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}\circ\Phi=\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)\circ\mathscr{D}\,.

In this manner, we arrive at a natural model of groupoidal gauge symmetry of the configuration bundle of the gauge(d) field theory-to-be.

Definition 3.14
.

Adopt the notation of Prop.
3.13
. We call the subgroup
{\rm im}\,\mathscr{F}_{*}\subset{\rm Aut}_{{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)}(\mathscr{F})
the
shadow automorphism group
, and its elements –
shadow automorphisms
. Upon restriction to
{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})\subset{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})
, we obtain the
shadow gauge group

\displaystyle{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{F}):=\mathscr{F}_{*}\bigl({\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})\bigr)\,,

whose elements are termed
shadow gauge transformations
.

A neat closure of the intrinsically (bi-)Lie-groupoidal model of gauge symmetry systematically reconstructed in our hitherto considerations, in the spirit of Ehresmann’s original work
[
Ehr50
]
(see also:
[
Pra07
]
), calls for one last

Definition 3.15
.

Adopt the notation of Thm.
3.6
. A bisection
\beta
of the Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid

Comparison of local data of
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant automorphisms of the principaloid bundle with those of
\pi
-projectable bisections of the corresponding Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid now yields

Theorem 3.16
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.15
and Prop.
3.13
. There is a canonical group isomorphism

\displaystyle\beta_{\cdot}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }{\rm Bisec}_{\pi}\bigl({\rm At}(\mathscr{P})\bigr)\,,

which restricts to a group isomorphism

\displaystyle{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})\cong{\rm Bisec}_{\pi}({\rm Ad}(\mathscr{P}))

between the respective subgroups. The former isomorphism renders commutative the following diagram

(3.31)

Example 3.18
.

Automorphisms of the Ehresmann principaloid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
-bundle from Ex.
3.9
are the standard
{\rm G}
-equivariant bundle automorphisms of
P
, in bijection with (all) bisections of the Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(P)
.

Example 3.19
.

Automorphisms of the Cartan principaloid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
-bundle
P\times M
from Ex.
3.10
are usually not considered in all generality, for the same reason as that given for the absence of the Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(P\times M)
in the literature. Instead, distinguished automorphisms of
P\times M
are induced from those of
P
, represented by the underlying Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(P)
, which acts on the first cartesian factor in
P\times M
. The action automatically commutes with the right action of the structure groupoid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
, the latter reducing to the right defining action of the structure group
{\rm G}
on that factor, and so it descends to the shadow
P\times_{\lambda}M
. Once more, we end up with the reduced structure group
\iota({\rm G})\subsetneq{\rm Bisec}({\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M)
.

Remark 3.20
.

We may invoke, once more, the construction of the universal principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
{\rm E}\mathscr{G}\to{\rm B}\mathscr{G}
from
[
AC11
]
, recalled in sufficient generality at the end of Sec.
2
, to justify the interpretation of the gauge principle employing all inequivalent principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundles
\mathscr{D}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{P}\to\mathscr{F}
in
{\rm{\bf Man}}/\Sigma
as a method of constructing an effective model of a field theory with configuration bundle
M//\mathscr{G}
over a given spacetime
\Sigma
in keeping with the principle of homogeneity. This last aspect of the construction advocated in
[
SS25
]
and in the present paper deserves an extra comment: If we were to adopt as the prototype of the present generalisation Ehresmann’s construction of the abstract bundle of gauges (
2.1
) (resp. (
2.13
)) instead of Cartan’s mixing construction (
2.4
) (resp. (
2.15
)) of
gauges-in-realisation, fibred over the space of internal degrees of freedom
, we might be led to identify the base of the principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundle with the spacetime of the field theory under construction—this is the case for applications of the old construct, due to MacKenzie, Moerdijk and Mrčun, of a principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundle, introduced as a mathematical model underlying the gauge principle for groupoidal symmetries. The important feature of this construct which distinguishes it from the principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle (and the attendant shadow bundle) is the violation of the aforementioned principle of homogeneity in general. Indeed, as demonstrated in
[
MM03
]
, every principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundle is locally trivialisable, with the local model given by the canonical principal
\mathscr{G}
-bundle—the unit bundle from Ex.
B.29
. However, the latter is, in general, only a surjective submersion, without a typical fibre, as its local fibres are
t
-fibres of
\mathscr{G}
, and it is easy to find Lie groupoids with pairwise non-diffeomorphic
t
-fibres. A simple example is provided by a full subgroupoid of an action groupoid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
obtained by the removal of some, but not all points from some
{\rm G}
-orbits.

3.3.
The connections, and gauge fields

The principle of
\mathscr{G}
-equivariance can be lifted coherently to the tangent of the principaloid bundle, whereby an adaptation of the notion of connection arises which completes Ehresmann’s construction in the present Lie-groupoidal setting.

Definition 3.21
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.1
. A (compatible)
connection
on a principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}
is an Ehresmann connection
{\rm T}\mathscr{P}={\rm V}\mathscr{P}\oplus{\rm H}\mathscr{P}
with a
\mathscr{G}
-invariant horizontal distribution
{\rm H}\mathscr{P}\subset{\rm ker}\,{\rm T}\mu
. In other words, for every
g\in\mathscr{G}
and
p\in\mu^{-1}(\{t(g)\})
, the horizontal distribution satisfies

(3.33)

\displaystyle{\rm T}_{p}\varrho_{g}({\rm H}_{p}\mathscr{P})={\rm H}_{\varrho_{g}(p)}\mathscr{P}\,,

where
\varrho_{g}(p)\equiv\varrho(p,g)
.

Equivalently, and conveniently from the field-theoretic point of view, we may work with smooth families of
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant projectors onto the vertical.

Definition 3.22
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.1
. A (compatible)
connection 1-form
on
\mathscr{P}
is a
{\rm V}\mathscr{P}
-valued 1-form
\Theta\in\Omega^{1}(\mathscr{P},{\rm V}\mathscr{P})\equiv\Gamma({\rm T}^{*}\mathscr{P}\otimes{\rm V}\mathscr{P})

such that, when viewed as an element in
{\rm End}{({\rm T}\mathscr{P})}
:

(GC1)

\Theta\big|_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}={\rm id}_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}
(a projection onto
{\rm V}\mathscr{P}
);

(GC2)

{\rm T}\mu\circ\Theta={\rm T}\mu
(kernel inclusion);

(GC3)

{\rm T}\varrho\circ(\Theta\times{\rm id}_{{\rm T}\mathscr{G}})\big|_{{\rm T}(\mathscr{P}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\,\mathscr{G})}=\Theta\circ{\rm T}\varrho
(
\mathscr{G}
-equivariance).

We have the anticipated

Proposition 3.23
.

Connections on a principaloid bundle are in a one-to-one correspondence with connection 1-forms on it.

With the help of the standard construction using a smooth partition of unity associated with the trivialising cover of the base of the principaloid bundle, we readily establish

Theorem 3.24
.

On every principaloid bundle, there exists a connection.

Similarly as in the case of automorphisms, building the principle of
\mathscr{G}
-equivariance into the definition of the connection enables us to employ the classic Kobayashi–Nomizu mechanism
[
KN63
]
to descend the connection to the shadow.

Proposition/Definition 3.25
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.21
. A connection on a principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
canonically induces an Ehresmann connection on
\mathscr{F}
along the sitting-duck map
\mathscr{D}
as

(3.34)

\displaystyle{\rm T}\mathscr{F}={\rm V}\mathscr{F}\oplus{\rm H}\mathscr{F}\,,\qquad\qquad{\rm V}\mathscr{F}={\rm T}\mathscr{D}({\rm V}\mathscr{P})\,,\qquad{\rm H}\mathscr{F}={\rm T}\mathscr{D}({\rm H}\mathscr{P})\,.

We call it the
shadow connection
on
\mathscr{F}
.

Once more, we have the equivalent description in terms of a smooth family of projectors.

Definition 3.26
.

Adopt the notation of Prop.
3.25
and Thm.
3.3
. Given a connection
{\rm T}\mathscr{P}={\rm V}\mathscr{P}\oplus{\rm H}\mathscr{P}
on
\mathscr{P}
and the corresponding shadow connection
{\rm T}\mathscr{F}={\rm V}\mathscr{F}\oplus{\rm T}\mathscr{D}({\rm H}\mathscr{P})
on
\mathscr{F}
, the
shadow connection 1-form
on
\mathscr{F}
is a
{\rm V}\mathscr{F}
-valued 1-form
\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}\in\Omega^{1}(\mathscr{F},{\rm V}\mathscr{F})\equiv\Gamma({\rm T}^{*}\mathscr{F}\otimes{\rm V}\mathscr{F})
with the property
{\rm T}\mathscr{D}({\rm H}\mathscr{P})={\rm ker}\,\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}
.

A simple structural relation between the two families of projectors—instrumental in establishing the physically all-important gauge-covariance property of the verticalised derivative on
\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
, to be reviewed shortly—is captured by

Proposition 3.27
.

The shadow connection 1-form from Def.
3.26
is uniquely determined by the identity

\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}\circ{\rm T}\mathscr{D}={\rm T}\mathscr{D}\circ\Theta\,.

The key field-theoretic rôle of a principal connection is that of a source of a background gauge field coupling to various charged-matter fields. A suitable adaptation of the former notion, taking into account the fibre bundle behind the Lie algebra
\Gamma_{\rm c}(\mathscr{E})
of the structure group
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
under consideration (see: Thm.
B.39
), is provided in

Definition 3.28
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
B.18
and
B.19
, of Cor.
3.2
, and of Ex.
B.44
. Let
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
be a Lie groupoid, and let
\mathscr{E}
be its tangent algebroid.
Local connection data
on a principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}
over
\Sigma
from Def.
3.1
are an assignment, to elements of a trivialising cover
\mathcal{O}\equiv\{O_{i}\}_{i\in I}
of
\Sigma
, of
{\rm T}O_{i}
-foliated
{\rm pr}_{2}^{*}\mathscr{E}
-valued 1-forms
A_{i}
on
O_{i}\times M
,
A_{i}\in\Gamma({\rm pr}_{1}^{*}{\rm T}^{*}O_{i}\otimes{\rm pr}_{2}^{*}\mathscr{E})
, subject, over double intersections
O_{ij}\ni\sigma
, to the following
gluing law
:

(3.35)

\displaystyle A_{i}\bigl(\sigma,t_{*}\bigl(\beta_{ij}(\sigma)\bigr)(m)\bigr)={\rm T}_{{\rm Id}_{m}}C_{\beta_{ij}(\sigma)}\circ A_{j}(\sigma,m)+\theta_{\rm R}\circ{\rm T}_{\sigma}\widetilde{\beta}{}_{ij}(\cdot,m)\,,

expressed in terms of smooth maps

(3.36)

\displaystyle\widetilde{\beta}{}_{ij}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{ij}\times M\longrightarrow\mathscr{G},\ (\sigma,m)\longmapsto\beta_{ij}(\sigma)(m)\,,

using the transition 1-cocycle
\{\beta_{ij}\}_{i,j\in I}
of
\mathscr{P}
, and the right-invariant Maurer–Cartan form
\theta_{\rm R}
on
\mathscr{G}
(see: Ex.
B.44
). The 1-forms are termed
local gauge fields
.

A structural link between the two notions is established in

Theorem 3.29
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.22
and
3.28
. For every principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}
, a connection 1-form determines local connection data, and vice versa. The relation between the two is given by the formula

(3.37)

\displaystyle\bigl(\mathscr{P}\tau_{i}^{-1\,*}\Theta\bigr)(\sigma,g)={\rm id}_{{\rm T}\mathscr{G}}\big|_{g}-{\rm T}_{{\rm Id}_{t(g)}}r_{g}\circ A_{i}\bigl(\sigma,t(g)\bigr)\,,\qquad(\sigma,g)\in O_{i}\times\mathscr{G}\,.

The realisation of the geometric function of the connection—that is: covariantisation of derivatives of matter fields through their verticalisation—requires that automorphisms of the principaloid bundle be promoted to connection-preserving ones. This reasoning leads to

Definition 3.30
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.11
and
3.22
. Let
\mathscr{P}
be a principaloid bundle with a connection 1-form
\Theta\in\Omega^{1}(\mathscr{P},{\rm V}\mathscr{P})
. Given an automorphism
\Phi\in{\rm Aut}(\mathscr{P})
, we denote

(3.38)

\displaystyle\Theta^{\Phi}:=\Phi^{-1\,*}\Theta\equiv{\rm T}\Phi\circ\Theta\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}\in\Omega^{1}(\mathscr{P},{\rm V}\mathscr{P})\,.

Whenever
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
, the 1-form
\Theta^{\Phi}
is called a
gauge transform
of
\Theta
.

The definition implies a simple behaviour of the shadow connection under gauge transformations.

Proposition 3.31
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.26
and
3.30
and Prop.
3.13
. For every gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
of a principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
with connection 1-form
\Theta
, the shadow connection 1-form
\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}\in\Omega^{1}(\mathscr{F},{\rm V}\mathscr{F})
satisfies the identity

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)^{*}\>\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}^{\Phi}=\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}\,,

in which
\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}^{\Phi}
is the shadow connection induced by the gauge transform
\Theta^{\Phi}
, and in which the pullback along
\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)
is explicitly given by

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)^{*}\>\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}^{\Phi}\equiv{\rm T}\bigl(\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)\bigr)^{-1}\circ\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}^{\Phi}\circ{\rm T}\bigl(\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)\bigr)\,.

That the above effects the desired promotion is documented by the following

Proposition 3.32
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.30
,
B.18
and
B.19
, of Cor.
3.2
, of Thm.
3.29
, and of Ex.
B.44
. For every gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
, the corresponding gauge transform
\Theta^{\Phi}
of the connection 1-form
\Theta
is, again, a connection 1-form on
\mathscr{P}
. Its local data
\{A^{\Phi}_{i}\}_{i\in I}
associated with a trivialising cover
\mathcal{O}\equiv\{O_{i}\}_{i\in I}
of
\Sigma
obey, over double intersections
O_{ij}\ni\sigma
, the same gluing law as their counterparts
\{A_{i}\}_{i\in I}
(see: (
3.35
)):

(3.39)

\displaystyle A^{\Phi}_{i}\bigl(\sigma,t_{*}\bigl(\beta_{ij}(\sigma)\bigr)(m)\bigr)={\rm T}_{{\rm Id}_{m}}C_{\beta_{ij}(\sigma)}\circ A^{\Phi}_{j}(\sigma,m)+\theta_{\rm R}\circ{\rm T}_{\sigma}\widetilde{\beta}{}_{ij}(\cdot,m)\,.

Proof.

We begin by checking the defining properties of a connection 1-form. Thus, using
{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}({\rm V}\mathscr{P})={\rm V}\mathscr{P}
, we find

\displaystyle\Theta^{\Phi}\big|_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}\equiv{\rm T}\Phi\circ\Theta\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}\big|_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}={\rm T}\Phi\circ{\rm id}_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}\big|_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}={\rm id}_{{\rm V}\mathscr{P}}\,.

Next, the
\lambda_{\mathscr{P}}
-invariance of the moment map
\mu
yields

\displaystyle{\rm T}\mu\circ\Theta^{\Phi}\equiv{\rm T}\bigl(\mu\circ\Phi\bigr)\circ\Theta\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}={\rm T}\mu\circ\Theta\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}={\rm T}\mu\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}={\rm T}\bigl(\mu\circ\Phi^{-1}\bigr)={\rm T}\mu\,.

Finally, we invoke the commutativity of
\lambda_{\mathscr{P}}
and
\varrho
to compute

(3.41)

\displaystyle\Theta^{\Phi}\circ{\rm T}\varrho

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\rm T}\Phi\circ\Theta\circ{\rm T}\bigl(\Phi^{-1}\circ\varrho\bigr)={\rm T}\Phi\circ\bigl(\Theta\circ{\rm T}\varrho\bigr)\circ\bigl({\rm T}\Phi^{-1}\times{\rm id}_{{\rm T}\mathscr{G}}\bigr)\big|_{{\rm T}(\mathscr{P}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\,\mathscr{G})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\rm T}\bigl(\Phi\circ\varrho\bigr)\circ\bigl(\bigl(\Theta\circ{\rm T}\Phi^{-1}\bigr)\times{\rm id}_{{\rm T}\mathscr{G}}\bigr)\big|_{{\rm T}(\mathscr{P}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\,\mathscr{G})}={\rm T}\varrho\circ\bigl(\Theta^{\Phi}\times{\rm id}_{{\rm T}\mathscr{G}}\bigr)\big|_{{\rm T}(\mathscr{P}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\,\mathscr{G})}\,.

The gluing law for the local data
\{A^{\Phi}_{i}\}_{i\in I}
of the thus established connection 1-form
\Theta^{\Phi}
is obtained from an analysis—conceptually identical to the one carried out for
\Theta
in
[
SS25
, Sec. 3.2]
—of the relations between the local presentations
\mathscr{P}\tau_{i}^{-1\,*}\Theta^{\Phi}
and
\mathscr{P}\tau_{j}^{-1\,*}\Theta^{\Phi}
over the intersections
O_{ij}\times\mathscr{G}
of their respective domains. Indeed, it is relative to the trivialisations
\mathscr{P}\tau_{i}
that the local data of the gauge transform
\Theta^{\Phi}
were derived
ibidem
. Thus, the dependence of the local presentation on the index of the cover comes solely from the pullback along the trivialisation, without any reference to
\Phi
.
∎

Putting the global content of Def.
3.30
in conjunction with the local content of Def.
3.28
, we discover the familiar affine-like behaviour of the local gauge field under redefinitions of gauge.

Proposition 3.33
.

Adopt the notation of Cor.
3.12
and Prop.
3.32
. For every gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
presented by local data
\gamma_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\to{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G}),\ i\in I
, local data
\{A_{i}^{\Phi}\}_{i\in I}
of
\Theta^{\Phi}
are related to those of
\Theta
by the following transformation law:

(3.42)

\displaystyle A_{i}^{\Phi}\bigl(\sigma,t_{*}\bigl(\gamma_{i}(\sigma)\bigr)(m)\bigr)={\rm T}_{{\rm Id}_{m}}C_{\gamma_{i}(\sigma)}\circ A_{i}(\sigma,m)+\theta_{\rm R}\circ{\rm T}_{\sigma}\widetilde{\gamma}{}_{i}(\cdot,m)\,,

written, for arbitrary
\sigma\in O_{i}
and
m\in M
, in terms of smooth maps

(3.43)

\displaystyle\widetilde{\gamma}{}_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\times M\longrightarrow\mathscr{G},\ (\sigma,m)\longmapsto\gamma_{i}(\sigma)(m)\,.

The last proposition provides us with a convenient local restatement of the gauge covariance of the (minimal) coupling between charged-matter and gauge fields modelled by the verticalised derivative, to be recalled next. As such, it proves to be instrumental in the analysis of a connection-aided configurational descent that is at the core of the present work.

Example 3.34
.

Compatible connections on the Ehresmann principaloid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
-bundle from Ex.
3.9
are standard principal connections. The corresponding
{\rm V}P
-valued connection 1-forms are usually replaced by
\mathfrak{g}
-valued 1-forms on
P
with the help of the trivialisation
{\rm V}P\cong P\times\mathfrak{g}
realised by the fundamental vector field
\mathcal{K}^{P}
of the defining action
r_{P}
.

Example 3.35
.

Compatible connections on the Cartan principaloid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
-bundle
P\times M
from Ex.
3.10
are usually not considered in all generality for the same reason as before (see: Ex.
3.10
). Instead, those encountered in the literature are induced—through pullback—from compatible connections on the principaloid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
-bundle
P
. As such, they automatically descend to the shadow
P\times_{\lambda}M
, see:
[
KN63
]
.

3.4.
The gauge-covariant derivative

A prototypical source of a coupling between charged-matter and gauge fields in a generic gauge(d) field theory is the verticalised derivation of the former, introduced in

Definition 3.36
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.26
. The
covariant derivative
of a section
\varphi\in\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
of the shadow bundle
\mathscr{F}
of a principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}

relative to
a connection 1-form
\Theta
on
\mathscr{P}
is the
C^{\infty}(\Sigma,{\mathbb{R}})
-linear mapping

(3.44)

\displaystyle\nabla^{\Theta}_{\cdot}\varphi\hskip-2.0pt:\Gamma({\rm T}\Sigma)\longrightarrow\Gamma(\varphi^{*}{\rm V}\mathscr{F}),\ \mathcal{V}\longmapsto\Theta_{\mathscr{F}}\circ{\rm T}\varphi(\mathcal{V})\equiv\nabla^{\Theta}_{\mathcal{V}}\varphi\,.

The prime rôle of the verticalisation, which consists in the covariantisation of the derivative relative to the action of the shadow gauge group, is documented in

Proposition 3.37
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
3.30
and
3.36
, and of Prop.
3.13
. For a section
\varphi\in\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
of the shadow bundle
\mathscr{F}
of a principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
, and a gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
of
\mathscr{P}
, let
\varphi^{\Phi}
denote the corresponding gauge transform of
\varphi
:

\displaystyle\varphi^{\Phi}\equiv\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)\circ\varphi\,.

The covariant derivative of
\varphi
relative to a connection 1-form
\Theta
on
\mathscr{P}
transforms
covariantly
as

\displaystyle\nabla^{\Theta^{\Phi}}_{\cdot}\bigl(\varphi^{\Phi}\bigr)={\rm T}\bigl(\mathscr{F}_{*}(\Phi)\bigr)\circ\nabla^{\Theta}_{\cdot}\varphi\,.

Remark 3.38
.

The last result illustrates an important structural feature of the gauge principle that emerges from our considerations: The simple transformational behaviour of the geometric coupling between the charged-matter and gauge fields hinges on the simultaneous redefinition of both: the differentiated matter field and the verticalising gauge field. We shall encounter certain complex variations on this universal theme in what follows.

The coupling referred to above becomes apparent in the local picture, in which, moreover, the tensorial transformation law under redefinitions of gauge acquires a form accessible to a field-theoretic construction which starts—as is usually the case (
e.g.
, in the approach to the gauging that employs gauge-symmetry defects modelling the twisted sector of the gauged field theory, see:
[
RS09
,
Sus12
,
Sus13
]
)—with geometric structures (tensors, higher-geometric objects
etc.
) on the configuration fibre
M
to be reduced.

Definition 3.39
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.36
and Thm.
3.29
. For every global section
\varphi\in\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
of the shadow
\mathscr{F}
of
\mathscr{P}
, with local data
\varphi_{i}:={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\varphi\big|_{O_{i}}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\to M,\ i\in I
in local trivialisations
\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{-1}(O_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}O_{i}\times M
induced by the
\mathscr{P}\tau_{i}
(see: the proof of Thm.
3.3
), we call the expression

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}:={\rm pr}_{2}\circ{\rm T}\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}\circ\nabla^{\Theta}_{\cdot}\varphi\big|_{O_{i}}

the
local presentation of the covariant derivative
of
\varphi

relative to

\Theta
(in trivialisation
\mathscr{F}\tau_{i}
).

Explicitly, we find

Proposition 3.40
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
3.39
, Cor.
3.12
and Prop.
3.32
. The local presentation of the covariant derivative of
\varphi\in\Gamma(\mathscr{F})
relative to
\Theta
takes the form

(3.45)

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}(\sigma)={\rm T}_{\sigma}\varphi_{i}-\alpha_{\mathscr{E}}\circ A_{i}\bigl(\sigma,\varphi_{i}(\sigma)\bigr)\,,\quad\sigma\in O_{i}\,.

Its components are subject, over double intersections
O_{ij}\ni\sigma
, to the following gluing law:

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}(\sigma)=T_{\varphi_{j}(\sigma)}t_{*}\bigl(\beta_{ij}(\sigma)\bigr)\circ\mathscr{D}^{A_{j}}\varphi_{j}(\sigma)\,,

and its tensorial behaviour under a gauge transformation
\Phi\in{\rm Gauge}(\mathscr{P})
with local presentation
\gamma_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:O_{i}\to{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G}),\ i\in I
is captured by the formula

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}^{A^{\Phi}_{i}}\varphi^{\Phi}_{i}(\sigma)=T_{\varphi_{i}(\sigma)}t_{*}\bigl(\gamma_{i}(\sigma)\bigr)\circ\mathscr{D}^{A_{i}}\varphi_{i}(\sigma)\,.

Proof.

Obvious.
∎

Example 3.41
.

The covariant derivative on sections of the shadow
P\times_{\lambda}M
of the Cartan principaloid
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
-bundle
P\times M
from Ex.
3.10
obtained from a distinguished connection 1-form on
P\times M
induced from a principal connection 1-form
\mathcal{A}\in\Omega^{1}(P)\otimes\mathfrak{g}
on the principaloid
\mathbf{B}{\rm G}
-bundle

is the standard Crittenden(-type) derivative, see:
[
Cri62
]
.

4.
Association: Reduction of the gauge group & proliferation of field species

The construction of a principaloid bundle, as reviewed in the previous section, exhibits a certain intrinsic rigidity, which may prove inconvenient from the perspective of both physical and mathematical model building: First of all, the definition of a principaloid bundle for a
given
Lie groupoid
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
, in which objects and morphisms are tied once and for all, does not come with a natural mechanism of reduction of the canonical structure group given by the group of (all) bisections of the structure groupoid, other than
ad hoc
and by hand. An obvious potential source of such reduction is the presence of an extra geometric structure on the groupoid,
e.g.
, a metric structure (see:
[
dHF18
]
), a symplectic structure (see:
[
Wei87
,
CDW87
]
), or an
n
-gerbe geometrising a (higher) gauge field that couples to the charge carried by a physical field (as in a
\sigma
-model), see: Sec.
7
below. One might wish to increase the modularity of the construction by separating the structure groupoid of the bundle of gauges from its structure group, encoded by the relevant gauge groupoid. This is, in fact, the standard situation encountered in the classic formulation of the gauge principle, in which—as observed in Ex.
3.19
—the gauge groupoid
{\rm At}(P)
provides a proper subset of the set of (
\pi
-projectable) bisections of the Ehresmann–Atiyah groupoid
{\rm At}(P\times M)
of the principaloid bundle under consideration. Another structural problem ensues from the identification of the principaloid bundle as a source of the gauge field: Based on standard physical experience (see,
e.g.
: the Standard Model of particle physics), one would expect to be able to couple
the same
gauge field to multiple
distinct
charged-matter fields, each coming with its own configuration fibre. In the present setting, the type of the charged-matter field is frozen as
M
.

Below, we propose a geometric mechanism which resolves both issues without ever sacrificing the key advantage of the novel construction of
[
SS25
]
, which is the existence of a nontrivial fibration of symmetry over the configuration space of the field theory, modelled on the source resp. target map of the structure groupoid. The mechanism is inspired by and, in particular, subsumes the original Cartan(–Borel) mixing construction reviewed in Sec.
2
. It is gratifying to conclude, once it has been formulated in full detail, that it actually fits within the broad conceptual framework of the original definition of a principaloid bundle, which thus retains its status of an overarching construction, but now acquires some ‘fine’ structure, and, with it, greater modularity.

4.1.
The geometry of the associating construction

We begin by adapting the Cartan(–Borel) mixing construction to the present setting, in which the bundle of gauges has been chosen in the categorified form of a principaloid bundle.

Definition 4.1
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.30
. Let
\,\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 9.34244pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-9.34244pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}_{a}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M_{a}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\ a\in\{1,2\}

The next definition provides us with a useful refinement of the ‘raw’ definition above.

Definition 4.3
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
4.1
and
B.32
. Let
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 9.34244pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-9.34244pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}_{a}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M_{a}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\ a\in\{1,2\}
be Lie groupoids, let
(X_{1},\mu_{X_{1}},\lambda_{X_{1}})
be a left
\mathscr{G}_{1}
-module and let
(X_{2},\mu_{X_{2}},\varrho_{X_{2}})
be a right
\mathscr{G}_{2}
-module. Furthermore, let

Theorem 4.4
.

B.28
and Cor.
3.2

(X,\mu_{X},\lambda_{X})

\mathscr{G}
-module. Every principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle
\mathscr{P}
canonically induces a fibre bundle

with model

(4.5)

\displaystyle\Xi\cong\bigsqcup_{i\in I}\,\bigl(O_{i}\times X\bigr)/\sim_{B\lambda_{X\,\beta_{\cdot\cdot}}}\xrightarrow{\ \pi_{\Xi}\ }\Sigma,\ [(\sigma,x,i)]\longmapsto\sigma\,,

(4.6)

\displaystyle(\sigma_{2},j,x_{2})\sim(\sigma_{1},i,x_{1})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\sigma_{1},x_{1})=\bigl(\sigma_{2},B\lambda_{X}\bigl(\beta_{ij}(\sigma_{1}),x_{2}\bigr)\bigr)\,,

of
\mathscr{P}

{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
on
X

\lambda_{X}
