9.
The gauge anomaly, and inequivalent gaugings

The principle underlying our proposal for the connection-aided descent of the topological component of a prequantisable PAG
\sigma
-model to the shadow bundle is
\mathscr{G}
-equivariance. It was first assumed on the tensorial level, where it gave rise to a multiplicative BSS extension of the curvature of the Cheeger–Simons character in the DF amplitude, and was subsequently lifted to the higher-geometric object
\mathcal{G}
determining the latter as its holonomy. The requirement of the existence of the extra structure on
\mathcal{G}
is far from innocent, or structureless—indeed, in general, there is an obstruction to it, also known as the
gauge anomaly
, which admits a precise cohomological quantification. As usual in the theory of extensions of (algebro-)geometric structures, the cohomology containing the obstruction class also classifies—lower in the cohomology degree—inequivalent extensions, whose physical relevance hinges on the fact that they correspond to quantum-mechanically inequivalent gauged field theories. This justifies the attention devoted to a detailed study of the gauge anomaly in the present section, prior to formulating the definition of the gauged field theory in the case of a vanishing anomaly.

We begin our discussion with the simpler, tensorial component of the anomaly.

Definition 9.1
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
5.5
and
7.1
. Let
\mathscr{M}_{\sigma}
be a closed two-dimensional nonlinear
\sigma
-model with rigid-symmetry model
\,\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt

in

9.1.
The (large) gauge-anomaly classes

The second part of the proof of Thm.

, given in App.

\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}[A_{i}]
under arbitrary integrated (
i.e.
, large) gauge transformations with model

calls for the existence of the 1-isomorphism
\Upsilon

to the shadow

(H_{M},\rho,0)
in the form of a
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}

\mathcal{G}
. This leads us to

Definition 9.2
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
9.1
,
D.10
and
D.14
. Let
(H_{M},\rho,0)
be a multiplicative BSS extension of the curvature

which lifts the small gauge anomaly of

for

. Furthermore, let
\mathcal{G}\in\mathfrak{BGrb}_{\nabla}(M)
be a gerbe of curvature

in
\mathcal{A}_{\rm DF}

large gauge anomaly
of

for

on

On the first level, relevant to both: the gauge invariance and the descent to
\mathscr{F}
, the anomaly admits a neat higher-geometric presentation given in

Proposition 9.3
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
9.2
and Thm.
D.3
. The obstruction to the existence of a 1-isomorphism

is given by the isomorphism class

\displaystyle[t^{*}\mathcal{G}\otimes s^{*}\mathcal{G}^{*}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{-\rho}]\in\mathcal{W}^{3}(\mathscr{G},0)\cong H^{2}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\,.

Proof.

The vanishing of the curvature of
t^{*}\mathcal{G}\otimes s^{*}\mathcal{G}^{*}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{-\rho}
is implied by the existence of an extension
[(H_{M},\rho,0)]
of the class
[H_{M}]
of the curvature
H_{M}
of
\mathcal{G}
. The statement of the proposition now follows directly from Prop.
D.6
and Thm.
D.3
.
∎

Corollary 9.4
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
9.2
. Whenever the arrow manifold
\mathscr{G}
has

, the 1-isomorphism

From the second level of the anomaly onwards, that is—in the context of the descent, it is convenient to base the analysis on the adapted Čech–Deligne–Dupont hypercohomological description (relative to a sufficiently fine simplicial cover of the nerve
N_{\bullet}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
, in the sense of
[

), introduced in Def.

.

Proposition 9.5
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
9.2
and Prop.
D.13
. Assume given a 1-isomorphism
\Upsilon
, and let
p_{\Upsilon}\in A^{1}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})
represent the latter in the sense of Prop.
D.7
. The obstruction to the existence of the 2-isomorphism
\gamma
is—for
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
sufficiently fine—given by the class

\displaystyle[[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}\in\widehat{h}{}^{2}(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1))\,.

Proof.

Let
b\in A^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{0}})
respresent the gerbe
\mathcal{G}
in the sense of Prop.
D.7
. The existence of
\Upsilon
then means that—for
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
sufficiently fine—

\displaystyle-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(2)}_{(0)}b+(\rho\big|_{O^{(1)}_{i}},0,1)=D^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}\,,

with the 1-cochain
p_{\Upsilon}
defined manifestly up to the addition
p_{\Upsilon}\mapsto p_{\Upsilon}+p
of a 1-cocycle
p\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(1)}_{(1)}
.

In consequence of the homological nature of the Dupont operators, and of the multiplicativity of
\rho
, we then find

\displaystyle D^{(1)}_{(2)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(2)}_{(1)}D^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(2)}_{(1)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(2)}_{(0)}b+\bigl(\Delta^{(0,2)}_{(1)}\rho\big|_{O_{i}^{(1)}},0,0\bigr)=0\,,

and so
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)
defines a class

\displaystyle[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)]=[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}]+[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}][p]\in H^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G}_{2},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\,.

Every 1-cocycle
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)
represents the 1-isomorphism
({\rm m}^{*}\Upsilon^{-1}\otimes{\rm Id})\circ({\rm pr}_{2}^{*}\Upsilon\otimes{\rm Id})\circ{\rm pr}_{1}^{*}\Upsilon
, and so the existence of
\gamma
means that—for
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
sufficiently fine—

\displaystyle\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}(p_{\Upsilon}+p)=-D^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}

for some 0-cochain
f_{\gamma}\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
. Hence, it is the class
[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}]\in P_{\mathscr{G}}^{2}
up to corrections
[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}][p]\equiv\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}^{(1)}[p]
with
[p]\in H^{1}(\mathscr{G}_{1},{\rm U}(1))\equiv P_{\mathscr{G}}^{1}
arbitrary that quantifies the obstruction to the existence of
\gamma
. By construction, the class is a 2-cocycle,

\displaystyle\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}^{(2)}[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}]\equiv[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(2)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}]=0\,.

∎

Corollary 9.6
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
9.2
. If
\Upsilon
exists, and the manifold
\mathscr{G}_{2}
of pairs of composable arrows has
H_{1}(\mathscr{G}_{2})={\boldsymbol{1}}
, then the 2-isomorphism
\gamma
exists.

Proof.

The statement is a consequence of Props.
9.5
and
D.7
, taken in conjunction with the Universal Coefficient Theorem.
∎

The last level of the obstruction—that to the coherence of a
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure—is quantified in

Proposition 9.7
.

Adopt the assumptions and the notation of Def.
9.2
and Prop.
D.13
. Assume given a 1-isomorphism
\Upsilon
and a 2-isomorphism
\gamma
, and let
f_{\gamma}\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
represent the latter in the sense of Prop.
D.7
. The obstruction to the coherence of the 2-isomorphism
\gamma
, as expressed by identity (
D.19
), is—for
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
sufficiently fine—given by the class

\displaystyle[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}\in h^{3}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\,.

Proof.

Let
p_{\Upsilon}\in A^{1}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})
and
f_{\gamma}\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
represent the 1-isomorphism
\Upsilon
and the 2-isomorphism
\gamma
, respectively, in the sense of Prop.
D.7
, so that equality

(9.1)

\displaystyle\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}=-D^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}

holds true. Changing the representative of
p_{\Upsilon}
within its cohomology class (or, equivalently, changing the representative of the 2-isomorphism class
[\Upsilon]
) as
p_{\Upsilon}\mapsto p_{\Upsilon}+D^{(0)}_{(1)}h,\ h\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})
becomes reflected in a correction
f_{\gamma}\mapsto f_{\gamma}+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h
. Taking into account the extra freedom of correction
f_{\gamma}\mapsto f_{\gamma}+k,\ k\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}
, inscribed in (
9.1
), we conclude that
f_{\gamma}
is determined up to (and so can be corrected by) a replacement

\displaystyle f_{\gamma}\mapsto f_{\gamma}+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h+k,\ (h,k)\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})\times{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}\,.

We now obtain

\displaystyle\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}\bigl(f_{\gamma}+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h+k\bigr)=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}k\,,

with

\displaystyle D^{(0)}_{(3)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(2)}D^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(2)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{\Upsilon}=0\,,

which altogether infers that the quantitative measure of the obstruction to the coherence is
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(3)}
up to corrections
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}k
with
k\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}
arbitrary. However,
{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(n)}\equiv{\mathbb{H}}^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{n}},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{n}))={\mathbb{H}}^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{n},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{n}))
for
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
sufficiently fine, and so
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}\in H^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{3},{\rm U}(1))\equiv\Gamma^{3}_{\mathscr{G}}
and
k\in\Gamma^{2}_{\mathscr{G}}
in virtue of Prop.
D.2
. Moreover,
\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(3)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}\equiv\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(3)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}=0
, that is
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{\gamma}
is automatically a 3-cocycle, to be considered up to 3-coboundaries
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}k\equiv\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(2)}k
.
∎

Corollary 9.8

155.52577pt\raise-94.44028pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-2.31447pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 155.52577pt\raise-84.66331pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 218.36533pt\raise-113.32832pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{{\boldsymbol{0}}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}

of the ČDD bicomplex of
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
associated to
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
.

Proof.

Let
(\Upsilon_{a},\gamma_{a}),\ a\in\{1,2\}
be two
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structures on
\mathcal{G}\in\mathfrak{BGrb}_{\nabla}(M)
, represented by the respective 2-cochains
(p_{\Upsilon_{a}},f_{\gamma_{a}})\in A^{1}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})\oplus A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
. The difference 2-cochain

\displaystyle(p_{1,2},f_{1,2}):=(p_{\Upsilon_{2}}-p_{\Upsilon_{1}},f_{\gamma_{2}}-f_{\gamma_{1}})

satisfies the equations

\displaystyle D^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{1,2}=0\,,\qquad\qquad\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p_{1,2}=-D^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{1,2}\,,\qquad\qquad\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f_{1,2}=0\,,

which identify
(p_{1,2},f_{1,2})
as a 2-cocycle in the total complex of
\mathcal{J}
,

\displaystyle\nabla_{(2)}(0,p_{1,2},f_{1,2})=0\,.

In the light of Def.
D.14
, the
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structures represented by the 2-cochains
(p_{\Upsilon_{a}},f_{\gamma_{a}})
are
\mathscr{G}
-equivariantly isomorphic if there exist

•

a 1-cochain
a_{1,2}\in A^{1}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{0}})
representing a 1-automorphism
\Phi\hskip-2.0pt:\mathcal{G}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathcal{G}
, and

•

a 0-cochain
h_{1,2}\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})
representing a (coherent) 2-isomorphism
\varphi\hskip-2.0pt:(d^{(1)*}_{1}\Phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rho}})\circ\Upsilon_{1}\overset{\cong}{\Longrightarrow}\Upsilon_{2}\circ d^{(1)*}_{0}\Phi
.

The two definitions translate into identities

\displaystyle-D^{(1)}_{(0)}a_{1,2}=0\,,\qquad\qquad p_{\Upsilon_{1}}-d^{(1)*}_{1}a_{1,2}+D^{(0)}_{(1)}h_{1,2}=p_{\Upsilon_{2}}-d^{(1)*}_{0}a_{1,2}\,,

which are to be augmented by an identity expressing the coherence condition (
D.20
):

\displaystyle d^{(2)*}_{1}h_{1,2}+f_{\gamma_{1}}=f_{\gamma_{2}}+d^{(2)*}_{0}h_{1,2}+d^{(2)*}_{2}h_{1,2}\,.

Altogether, then, an equivalence between the two
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structures, whenever it exists, boils down to the triviality of the difference 2-cochain
(p_{1,2},f_{1,2})
in the cohomology of
\mathcal{J}
, with the primitive given by the 1-cochain
(a_{1,2},h_{1,2})
,

\displaystyle(0,p_{1,2},f_{1,2})=\nabla_{(1)}(a_{1,2},h_{1,2})\,.

This completes the proof.
∎

While precise, the above quantification is also somewhat opaque and unwieldy, because—unlike that of the anomaly—it does not seem to be related to the topology of the simplicial manifold
N_{\bullet}(\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt)
in a tractable manner, through, say, the Universal Coefficient Theorem. This apparent shortcoming is at least partialy alleviated by the following observation, which refines and generalises the original, motivating one from
[
GSW10
]
.

Proposition 9.10
.

Adopt the assumptions and the notation of Prop.
9.9
. There exists a canonical abelian-group homomorphism

\displaystyle\chi\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{H}}^{2}(\mathcal{J})\longrightarrow\widehat{h}{}^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)

with

\displaystyle{\rm ker}\,\chi\cong h^{2}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)

and

\displaystyle{\rm im}\,\chi=\bigl\{\ [[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}\in\widehat{h}{}^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\quad|\quad\exists f\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})\hskip-2.0pt:D^{(0)}_{(2)}f=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p\quad\land\quad[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}=0\ \bigr\}\,.

Proof.

Consider a 2-cochain
(p,f)\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(1)}_{(1)}\oplus A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
in
\mathcal{J}
which is closed,

\displaystyle\nabla_{(2)}(0,p,f)=0\,,

or, equivalently,

(9.2)

\displaystyle D^{(1)}_{(1)}p=0\,,\qquad\qquad\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p=-D^{(0)}_{(2)}f\,,\qquad\qquad\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f=0\,.

For a sufficiently fine cover
\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{\bullet}}
, the class
[p]\in{\mathbb{H}}^{1}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{1}))={\mathbb{H}}^{1}(\mathscr{G}_{1},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{1}))\cong H^{1}(\mathscr{G}_{1},{\rm U}(1))\equiv P^{1}_{\mathscr{G}}
(see: Prop.
D.2
) satisfies

\displaystyle\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}^{(1)}[p]\equiv[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}][p]=[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p]=0\,,

and so the map

\displaystyle{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}(\mathcal{J})\longrightarrow\widehat{h}{}^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr),\ (p,f)\longmapsto[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}

is well-defined. Whenever the 2-cocycle
(p,f)
is a 2-coboundary,
i.e.
, there exists
(a,h)\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(1)}_{(0)}\oplus A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{1}})
such that

\displaystyle(0,p,f)=\nabla_{(1)}(a,h)\,,

or, in other words,

\displaystyle p=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a+D^{(0)}_{(1)}h\,,\qquad\qquad f=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h\,,\qquad\qquad D^{(1)}_{(0)}a=0\,,

we obtain

\displaystyle[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}=[[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}=[[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}][a]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}=0\,.

Hence, the above map induces the sought-after map in cohomology:

\displaystyle\chi\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{H}}^{2}(\mathcal{J})\longrightarrow\widehat{h}{}^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr),\ [(p,f)]_{\nabla}\longmapsto[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}

We begin the analysis of
\chi
with the examination of its kernel. Given
\chi([(p,f)]_{\nabla})=0
, we have
[p]=\widehat{\delta}{}^{(0)}_{\mathscr{G}}[a]\equiv[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a]
for some
a\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(1)}_{(0)}
, and hence there exists
h\in A^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{1})
such that
p-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a=D^{(0)}_{(1)}h
. This further implies
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}D^{(0)}_{(1)}h=D^{(0)}_{(2)}\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h
, which in virtue of the cocyclicity (
9.2
) of
(p,f)
yields (again, for a sufficiently fine cover)

\displaystyle k(p,f):=f+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}\equiv{\mathbb{H}}^{0}\bigl(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{2})\bigr)={\mathbb{H}}^{0}\bigl(\mathscr{G}_{2},\mathscr{D}^{\bullet}(2;\mathscr{G}_{2})\bigr)\cong H^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{2},{\rm U}(1))\equiv\Gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{2}\,,

see: Prop.
D.2
. Thus,

\displaystyle[(p,f)]_{\nabla}=[(\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a+D^{(0)}_{(1)}h,-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h+k(p,f))]_{\nabla}\equiv[(0,k)+\nabla_{(1)}(a,h)]_{\nabla}=[(0,k(p,f))]_{\nabla}\,.

Furthermore,
\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(2)}k(p,f)=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f=0

(again, in consequence of the cocyclicity of
(p,f)
), and allowed corrections
h\mapsto h+h_{0}
with
h_{0}\in{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}\equiv\Gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{2}\,
induce shifts
k(p,f)\mapsto k(p,f)+\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(1)}h_{0}
. Altogether, this indicates that we are dealing with a map
(p,f)\mapsto[k(p,f)]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}\in h^{2}(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1))
. The map is additive, and so upon checking that it sends
\nabla
-coboundries to
0
,

\displaystyle[k(\nabla_{(1)}(a,h))]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}\equiv[k(\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(0)}a+D^{(0)}_{(1)}h,-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h)]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}=[-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h+\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}(h+h_{0})]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}\equiv 0\,,

we thus obtain a well-defined homomorphism

\displaystyle\widehat{\iota}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm ker}\,\chi\longrightarrow h^{2}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr),\ [(p,f)]_{\nabla}\longmapsto[k(p,f)]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}\,.

Note that
[k]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}=0
implies the existence of
h\in\Gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{1}\equiv H^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{1},{\rm U}(1))\equiv{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(1)}
such that
k=\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(1)}h\equiv\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h
, and then
[(0,k)]_{\nabla}=[(0,\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h)]_{\nabla}\equiv[(-D^{(0)}_{(1)}h,\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(1)}h)]_{\nabla}\equiv[\nabla_{(1)}(0,-h)]_{\nabla}=0
. Hence,
\widehat{\iota}
is injective. Since it is also manifestly surjective, we conclude that it is the anticipated isomorphism

\displaystyle\widehat{\iota}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm ker}\,\chi\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }h^{2}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\,.

We complete the proof by investigating the structure of
{\rm im}\,\chi
. By construction,

\displaystyle{\rm im}\,\chi\subset\bigl\{\ [[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}\in\widehat{h}{}^{1}\bigl(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1)\bigr)\quad|\quad\exists f\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})\hskip-2.0pt:D^{(0)}_{(2)}f=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p\quad\land\quad[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}=0\ \bigr\}\,,

see: (
9.2
), and so it remains to verify that every element of the set on the right-hand side of the above relation can be obtained from some 2-cocycle
(p,f)\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}(\mathcal{J})
. Consider such
[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}\in\widehat{h}{}^{1}(\mathscr{G},{\rm U}(1))
, and fix the corresponding
f\in A^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{G}_{2}})
. The identity
[\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f]_{\delta_{\mathscr{G}}}=0
implies the existence of
k\in\Gamma^{2}_{\mathscr{G}}\equiv H^{0}(\mathscr{G}_{2},{\rm U}(1))\equiv{\rm ker}\,D^{(0)}_{(2)}
such that
\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f=\delta_{\mathscr{G}}^{(2)}k\equiv\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}k
, and so we arrive at the complete list of equations

\displaystyle D^{(1)}_{(1)}p=0\,,\qquad\qquad D^{(0)}_{(2)}f=-\underline{\Delta}{}^{(1)}_{(1)}p\,,\qquad\qquad\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}f=\underline{\Delta}{}^{(0)}_{(2)}k\,,\qquad\qquad D^{(0)}_{(2)}k=0

describing
[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}
. The shifted 2-cochain
(p^{\prime},f^{\prime}):=(p,f)-(0,k)
of
\mathcal{J}
is closed, and yields
\chi([(p^{\prime},f^{\prime})])=[[p]]_{\widehat{\delta}{}_{\mathscr{G}}}
, as desired.
∎

Example 9.11
.

The closed WZNW
\sigma
-model
\mathscr{M}_{\sigma}
from Ex.
5.6
has a vanishing small gauge anomaly for the rigid-symmetry model given by the AMM groupoid from Ex.
7.13
. Moreover, the 2-connectedness of the group manifold
{\rm G}
ensures—in virtue of Cors.
9.4
,
9.6
, and
9.8
—that there is no large gauge anomaly, either. The two cochain complexes from Prop.
D.13
trivialise in the present setting, and hence so does the classifying cohomology group
{\mathbb{H}}^{2}(\mathcal{J})\cong{\rm ker}\,\chi={\boldsymbol{1}}
.

10.
The gauged PAG
\sigma
-model

In the present section, we put together the findings of Secs.
7
and
8
—under the assuption that the gauge anomalies described in Sec.
9
vanish—and define a gauged field theory canonically induced from the PAG
\sigma
-model from Def.
5.1
, with the configuration bundle given by the shadow of an arbitrary principaloid bundle with the structure group fully reduced according to Assumption (R) from p.
7
.

Theorem 10.1
.

Adopt the notation of Defs.
5.5
,
8.4
, and
8.7
. Consider a PAG
\sigma
-model
\mathscr{M}_{\sigma}
with rigid-symmetry model

Remark 10.3
.

The following general comment is well due at this stage: It might seem that we are not gauging (the target action of)
\mathscr{G}
itself, but merely (the shadow action of)
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
—or, indeed, its reduction (which, however, might be viewed tentatively as coming from another structure groupoid through association). On the other hand, for
{\mathbb{B}}
-complete groupoids the distinction becomes immaterial, and so—in view of the remark from p.
8
—we may safely regard the gauging as that of the monodromy groupoid of the tangent algebroid (and so of the linearised rigid symmetries) of the given Lie groupoid.

.

11.
The symplectic scenario: An emergent Poisson
\sigma
-model

Among the multitude of Lie groupoids—regarded here as field-theoretic rigid-symmetry models–there is a class that has attracted considerable attention over the years, and can therefore provide us with a concrete realisation of the abstract construction contemplated in the present work, to wit: symplectic groupoids, as defined in
[

induced from the Poisson bracket
\{\cdot,\cdot\}_{\Pi}
on

through the identification

as

\displaystyle[{\rm d}f_{1}(e),{\rm d}f_{2}(e)]^{*}:={\rm d}\{f_{1},f_{2}\}_{\Pi}(e)\,.

The Poisson bracket on
C^{\infty}({\rm G}^{*},{\mathbb{R}})
is the unique one whose linearisation at the group unit

\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 13.20836pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-13.20836pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{(\mathscr{L}\mathscr{W}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 27.43472pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 27.43472pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 27.43472pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\rm G}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\omega_{\mathscr{L}\mathscr{W}})
(see: Ex.

Finally, let us note—by way of a closing observation—that the obstruction analysis of Sec.

∎

Our analysis of the symplectic scenario places the long-known topological field theory in an essentially new perspective: Depending on the preferred point of view, we may either view the original Poisson
\sigma
-model of
[
Ike94
,
SS94
]
as a topological gauge field theory with an intrinsically non-integrable (in general) Lie-algebroidal gauge symmetry, or we may regard the coaugmentation of Def.
11.3
as an appropriate completion of the original field theory in which the linearised Lie-groupoidal symmetry has been integrated, and—at the same time—acces to configuration (shadow) bundles with nontrivial topology has been gained. In the former case, the
\mathcal{G}
-coaugmented Poisson
\sigma
-model is to be seen as an extension of the original field theory, conceptually independent of the original one, endowed with a richer and topologically more intricate categorified gauge symmetry. In the latter case, it acquires the status of the complete and canonically prequantisable—through the gerbe-theoretic transgression of
[
Gaw88
]
—formulation of the ancestor field theory, with
effectively Poisson-reduced
internal degrees of freedom
M//\mathscr{G}
. The latter point of view, which identifies the Poisson
\sigma
-model with the topological sector of a PAG
\sigma
-model with the target space given by the object manifold of a symplectic groupoid, and with the corresponding lagrangean bisections gauged, opens an avenue to the application of techniques of gerbe theory in the construction and cohomological classification of prequantisable boundary states and more general defects in the
\mathcal{G}
-coaugmented Poisson
\sigma
-model. For a flat coaugmentation, we thus obtain a powerful (higher-)geometric criterion distinguishing branes and bi-branes (in the language of
[
FSW08
]
and
[
RS09
]
). In any event, the 2
d
gauged field theory calls for an in-depth investigation, which is currently underway.

12.
Summary and Outlook

.

We have investigated the gauging of rigid field-theoretic symmetries modelled on an arbitrary Lie groupoid
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
with the object manifold
M
given by the configuration fibre of the field theory of interest. In so doing, we have considered the recently proposed principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundles with (compatible) connection
(\mathscr{P},\Theta)
and their Godement shadows
(\mathscr{F},\Theta_{\mathscr{F}})
(Sec.
3
) as a natural point of departure and the main building block of the proposed construction—a source of a local Lie algebroid-valued gauge field (the former), and a model of the configuration bundle of the field theory with the groupoidal symmetry gauged (the latter). As argued in Sec.
2
, the gauging procedure is to be understood as a way to model dynamics with a configuration fibre reduced to the characteristic foliation
M//\mathscr{G}
of the groupoid, of particular relevance in the absence of a smooth structure on the latter orbispace. In our construction, grounded in the greater comprehensiveness of the categorified model of symmetry in contemporary field theory, we have drawn inspiration from a systematic reformulation of the classical gauge principle—originally worked out for action groupoids
{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M
associated with smooth (Lie-)group actions
\lambda
on the configuration fibre—in the language of Lie groupoids, their associated Lie groups of global bisections, and principal bibundles (Sec.
2
).

As the first new result, we have worked out a groupoidal counterpart of Cartan’s mixing construction, in which the fibering of the symmetry model over the space of internal degrees of freedom of the field theory—in the slice
{\rm{\bf Bun}}(\Sigma)/\Sigma
over a given spacetime
\Sigma
—has been generalised from the previously studied canonical one, given by the target map of the structure groupoid
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
, to its pullback along the moment map
\mu_{X}\hskip-2.0pt:X\to M
of an arbitrary groupoid module
(X,\mu_{X},\lambda_{X})
(Sec.
4
). The thus obtained bundle associated to a given principaloid bundle
\mathscr{P}
by the action
\lambda_{X}
of
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
has been interpreted as a special example of a principaloid
\mathscr{G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda_{X}}X
-bundle—one with a structure group reduced to the image of that of
\mathscr{P}
—
i.e.
, of
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
—along a homomorphism canonically induced by
\mu_{X}
. The reduction is anticipated (and, indeed, has been demonstrated, in Sec.
7
) to be necessary in the presence of extra differential-geometric structure on the configuration fibre of the field theory—such as a metric tensor or a higher-geometric object (a bundle, a gerbe,
etc.
)—and thus justifies the abstract construction. Another key rationale for the latter is the possibility it offers to couple multiple charged-matter fields, modelled on global sections of bundles associated to
\mathscr{P}
, to a single gauge field, encoded by the connection
\Theta
on
\mathscr{P}
, through a groupoidal variant of the Crittenden construction of an associated connection.

The second key result of the present paper is the gauging prescription for Lie-groupoidal rigid symmetries in the two-dimensional Polyakov–Alvarez–Gawȩdzki
\sigma
-model with the topological Wess–Zumino term in the Dirac–Feynman amplitude given by a degree-3 Cheeger–Simons differential character—the surface holonomy of a gerbe
\mathcal{G}
over the metric target space
(M,{\rm g}_{M})
. The symmetry has been assumed to manifest itself as the invariance of the target metric
{\rm g}_{M}
and—independently—of the isomorphism class of the target gerbe
\mathcal{G}
under the target action
t_{*}
of
distinguished
bisections of
\mathscr{G}
on
M
. More specifically, a consistent implementation of the symmetry has been shown—in Sec.
7
---to naturally

\mathscr{F}

\Theta
(Sec.

), an idea largely inspired by and generalising the classic group-symmetry prototype worked out in
[
GSW10
]
(Sec.
6
). In the metric sector, a sheaf-theoretic descent has been attained through the usual minimal coupling,
i.e.
, through the evaluation of the metric tensor on
\Theta

8.8
). In the topological sector, the augmentation requisite for a fully fledged 2-stacky descent has been found to be mediated by the 2-comomentum component of the Spencer pair of the multiplicative extension
\rho
, and based on the assumption of a coherent prequantisation of the latter in the form of a
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure on the target gerbe
\mathcal{G}
(Thm.
8.6
). An exhaustive cohomological analysis of obstructions to the prequantisation, and a similar classification of inequivalent gaugings in the absence of such obstructions have been given in Sec.
9
—once more drawing heavily on the methodology and findings of
[
GSW10
]
. This part of our study has been crowned—in Sec.
10
—with the definition and the statement of gauge symmetry of the gauged PAG
\sigma
-model with the configuration bundle given by the shadow of an arbitrary principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle with the structure group reduced to
{\mathbb{B}}_{\sigma}(\mathscr{G})
as above (Thm.
10.1
).

The last result of our investigation is a novel conceptualisation of the distinguished two-dimensional topological field theory—the Poisson
\sigma
-model of
[
Ike94
,
SS94
]
—obtained as an intricate spin-off of a specialisation of the previous discussion of the gauging to the symplectic setting of
[
Wei87
,
CDW87
]
, and a subsequent far-reaching generalisation of the original field theory proposed in Sec.
11
. The specialisation—restricted to the topological sector of the PAG
\sigma
-model—consists in fixing the target space of the field theory in the form of a Poisson object manifold
(M,\Pi)
of a symplectic groupoid
(\mathscr{G},\omega)
, the latter being equipped with a multiplicative symplectic form
\omega\in Z^{2}_{\rm dR}(\mathscr{G})
. Remarkably, the lagrangean Dirac–Feynman amplitude of the classical Poisson
\sigma
-model has been recovered as the trivial Cheeger–Simons differential character augmenting an
\omega
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant gerbe
\mathcal{G}
over
M
in the manner proposed in Sec.
8
. In particular, the local gauge field coming from the connection
\Theta
on the underlying
symplectic
principaloid
(\mathscr{G},\omega)
-bundle—with the structure group reduced to the lagrangean group
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G},\omega)
of the structure groupoid—has been suitably identified with the
{\rm T}^{*}M
-valued gauge field of the Poisson
\sigma
-model. In the light of Thm.
8.6
, this has opened the possibility of extending the original definition of the Poisson
\sigma
-model to shadows of symplectic principaloid
(\mathscr{G},\omega)
-bundles of arbitrary topology (Def.
11.3
), and, simultaneously, of integrating their on-shell Lie-algebroidal gauge symmetries to off-shell Lie-groupoidal ones modelled on
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G},\omega)
(Thm.
11.4
). Topological obstructions to the extension, contingent upon the existence of the coaugmenting
\omega
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant gerbe
\mathcal{G}
, have been quantified in a specialisation of the former anomaly analysis (Prop.
11.6
). It has been observed that distinguished flat coaugmentations (
i.e.
, those with
\mathcal{G}
flat) leave the form—and so also the Lie-algebroidal interpretation—of the field equations of the original model unchanged.

The findings reported in the present work provide a solid body of evidence for the applicability and relevance in the rich context of field theory of the abstract notion of principaloid bundle proposed in
[
SS25
]
. They also prompt a number of follow-up questions, and chart directions for future research, of which we list a few in the closing paragraphs of this section.

(F1)

A natural continuation of the study initited herein is a reinterpretation of the gauging of the PAG
\sigma
-model in terms of topological gauge-symmetry defect networks carrying the data of a
\rho
-twisted
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant structure on the target gerbe, along the lines of the pioneering work
[
FSW08
,
RS09
]
and, in particular,
[
Sus12
,
Sus13
]
(see also:
[
Sus23
]
for a recent application in the supergeometric setting). Results of a work thus oriented are currently being written up and shall be published soon.

(F2)

Another obvious extension of our endeavour is a formulation of the gauging prescription in the presence of boundaries and more general defects in the field theory prior to the gauging, in structural analogy with the precursor project
[
GSW13
]
dedicated to Lie-group symmetries. This would entail,
i.a.
, the identification and examination of natural conditions for the compatibility of defects with bulk groupoidal symmetries discussed in the present paper. In the light of the analyses presented in
[
RS09
,
RS11
,
Sus22
]
, the theory of double Lie groupoids, originally advanced by Ehresmann in
[
Ehr63
]
, and later developed,
i.a.
, by Mackenzie in
[
Mac92
,
Mac00
]
, is expected to be of relevance.

(F3)

The cohomological nature of the non-tensorial term in the DF amplitude of the PAG
\sigma
-model invites further examination of the amenability to gauging of
weakly

\rho
-holonomic bisections:

\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{B}}{}_{\rho}(\mathscr{G}):=\{\ \beta\in{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\quad|\quad[\beta^{*}\rho]=0\in H^{k}(M)\ \}\supset{\mathbb{B}}_{\rho}(\mathscr{G})\,,

see: Rem.
7.3
. The findings of Crainic
et al.
on the relation between multiplicative
k
-forms on Lie groupoids and Spencer operators (see, in particular,
[
CS15
]
) are certain to play an instrumental rôle in this context.

(F4)

The definition of the PAG
\sigma
-model (and its higher-dimensional generalisations) uses Cheeger–Simons differential characters, which—while in a one-to-one correspondence with isoclasses of gerbes—provide us with a very particular, purely (homology-)algebraic description of the corresponding algebro-geometric objects. The latter may help to circumnavigate some technical complexities of the direct application of its higher-geometric counterpart developed by Murray
et al.
in the present work. Therefore, it seems apposite to inspect a reformulation of the hitherto work, as well as that proposed in the points (F1)-(F3) above, in terms of the axiomatic Cheeger–Simons cohomology, and in particular in (the Lerman–Malkin stacky rendering
[
LM08
,
LM09
]
of) its functorial Hopkins–Singer model
[
HS05
]
, which has been successfully employed in
[
Fil25
]
in the gauge analysis of the prototypical 1
d

\sigma
-model of dynamics of a charged massive probe.

(F5)

In all hitherto considerations, the Lie-algebroidal gauge field encoded by the connection 1-form on the principaloid
\mathscr{G}
-bundle has featured as a non-dynamical background in which (probe) charged-matter fields propagate. The formulation of a natural algebroidal Yang–Mills-type model of dynamics of the gauge field, inextricably entwined with the Higgs field (see: the discussion in Sec.
4.5
), is evidently required for the internal conistency of the theory, in which the gauge field should have sources of its curvature (
i.e.
, charges). Proposals for such models, valid in the simplified scenario in which the gauge field is globally smooth and the gauge symmetry is modelled on (smooth functions from spacetime into) a Lie algebroid have been known for more than two decades, see:
[
Str04
,
KS15
]
, and it is clear—with the concepts and techniques developed in
[
SS25
]
and in the present paper—how to generalise them to principaloid (and shadow) bundles of arbitrary topology, and for the corresponding integrated gauge-symmetry models. The relevant constructions are currently under investigation and shall be presented in near future.

(F6)

The previous point can be regarded as an ouverture to a more fundamental search for a universal gauge-field theory for principaloid bundles—
i.e.
, for the corresponding variant of the Chern–Weil theory—building on,
i.a.
, the work of Crainic
et al.
, see:
[
AC11
]
. Establishing a field-theoretic manifestation of the fundamental concept of Morita equivalence of Lie groupoids (see:
[
dH13
]
for a nice introduction to the subject) would also be of great interest, all the more so in the light of the conceptualisation of the gauging as configurational descent to the characteristic foliation
M//\mathscr{G}
.

(F7)

Besides modelling configurational reduction with respect to a Lie-groupoid action (as in the present paper), and exhibiting their autonomous Higgs-coupled dynamics (as in (F5)), Lie-algebroidal gauge fields are bound to enter models of dynamics of charged probes. Defining the latter calls for an understanding and explicit construction of holonomy and more general transport operators on principaloid bundles. It stands to reason that comomentum components of multiplicative forms, with their very tractable behaviour under the action of the (reduced) gauge group by the conjugation (in a local presentation), might be of use as candidate ‘trace’ maps on Lie algebroids. The coaugmentation mechanism uncovered in Sec.
11
in the setting of the Poisson
\sigma
-model also offers an interesting theoretical possibility.

(F8)

In the symplectic context, one natural line of development would be to invoke the well-studied identification of defects (resp. boundary states) in the PAG
\sigma
-model—derived in
[
RS09
]
—with gerbe bi-modules (resp. modules), and apply the bicategorial and higher-cohomological arsenal of gerbe theory
[
Ste00
,
Wal07a
]
, in a novel approach to the reconstruction and classification of prequantisable (bi-)branes in the gerbe-coaugmented Poisson
\sigma
-model, building upon the hitherto lagrangean-TFT developments
[
CF04
,
CF05
]
(see also:
[
Fal10
]
for a review). Given the correspondence between
\sigma
-models defects and symmetries/dualities of the 2
d
field theory, elaborated in
[
RS09
,
RS11
,
Sus11a
,
Sus22
]
, this opens an avenue to a higher-geometric and -categorial investigation of prequantisable dualities in this newly discovered environment. Its applications could be quite astounding, see,
e.g.
,
[
NW25
]
.

(F9)

Remaining in the context of dualities of Poisson
\sigma
-models, one would be tempted to examine the Lu–Weinstein construction from Ex.
11.5
(or, potentially, also its formal generalisation from
[
CF00b
]
) from the new vantage point offered by the gauging of symplectic-groupoidal symmetries in the coaugmented Poisson
\sigma
-model. Indeed, the groupoid

Given that the typical fibre
\mathscr{L}\mathscr{W}({\rm G},\Pi)
of
\mathscr{P}
is locally diffeomorphic to the product manifold
{\rm G}\times{\rm G}^{*}
, and equipped with a non-degenerate 2-form
\omega_{\mathscr{L}\mathscr{W}({\rm G},\Pi)}
(which admits—under obvious circumstances—a prequantisation to a Poincaré-type bundle), it is tempting to think of the above structure as an arena for various field-theoretic dualities—now amenable to gerbe-theoretic analysis, whenever prequantisable—formerly considered in the literature in the present Poisson–Lie setting, such as the duality between the Poisson
\sigma
-model with target
({\rm G}^{*},\Pi^{*})
and the fully gauged WZNW
\sigma
-model with target
{\rm G}

[
ASS95
,
FG02
]
(see: Ex.
10.4
), the open-closed duality between Poisson
\sigma
-models for the dual targets
({\rm G},\Pi)
and
({\rm G}^{*},\Pi^{*})

[
CFGA03
]
, or the intricate Poisson
T
-duality between the respective dynamical (PAG)
\sigma
-models
[
KŠ95
,
AKT96
]
.

Clearly, a systematic exploration of the physics of groupoidal gauge theory based on the notion of principaloid bundle and its Godement shadow, initiated in the present work, encompasses many conceptual and formal challenges. We hope to address them in our future work.

Appendix A
Generalities

In this appendix, we gather some general conventions and results used in the main text.

Convention A.1
.

Let
M_{a}
and
N_{a}
, with
a\in\{1,2\}
, be smooth manifolds and let
f_{a}\hskip-2.0pt:M_{a}\to N_{a}
be smooth maps. We write

\displaystyle f_{1}\times f_{2}\hskip-2.0pt:M_{1}\times M_{2}\longrightarrow N_{1}\times N_{2},\ (m_{1},m_{2})\longmapsto\bigl(f_{1}(m_{1}),f_{2}(m_{2})\bigr)\,.

Convention A.2
.

Let
M
and
N_{a}
, with
a\in\{1,2\}
, be smooth manifolds and let
f_{a}\hskip-2.0pt:M\to N_{a}
be smooth maps. We write

\displaystyle(f_{1},f_{2})\hskip-2.0pt:M\longrightarrow N_{1}\times N_{2},\ m\longmapsto\bigl(f_{1}(m),f_{2}(m)\bigr)\,.

Convention A.3
.

Let
N
and
M_{a}
, with
a\in\{1,2\}
, be smooth manifolds and let
f_{a}\hskip-2.0pt:M_{a}\to N
be smooth maps. We write

\displaystyle M_{1}\times_{N}M_{2}\equiv M_{1}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{f_{1}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{f_{2}}\hskip-2.0ptM_{2}=\bigl\{\ (m_{1},m_{2})\in M_{1}\times M_{2}\quad|\quad f_{1}(m_{1})=f_{2}(m_{2})\ \bigr\}\,.

Proposition A.4
.

Adopt the notation of Conv.
A.3
. Whenever one of the maps
f_{a}
is a surjective submersion,
M_{1}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{f_{1}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{f_{2}}\hskip-2.0ptM_{2}
is a smooth submanifold of
M_{1}\times M_{2}
.

Theorem A.5

(The Godement Criterion)
.

[
Ser06
,
Fer24
]

Let
M
be a smooth manifold and let
\sim
be an equivalence relation on M, with graph

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern There exists a smooth structure on the quotient

\displaystyle M//\sim=\{\ [m]_{\sim}\quad|\quad m\in M\ \}\,,

compatible with the quotient topology, and such that
\pi\hskip-2.0pt:M\longrightarrow M//\sim
is a submersion, iff the graph
\mathcal{R}_{\sim}
is a proper submanifold of
M\times M
and the restriction of the projection
{\rm pr}_{1}\hskip-2.0pt:M\times M\longrightarrow M
to
\mathcal{R}_{\sim}
is a submersion.

Convention A.6
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category with source
s
and target
t
. We shall write
A\in\mathcal{C}
if
A
belongs to the object class of
\mathcal{C}
, and
f\in\mathcal{C}(A,B)
if
f
belongs to the morphism class of
\mathcal{C}
, with
(s,t)(f)=(A,B)
.

Appendix B
Essential facts about Lie groupoids and algebroids

The present appendix contains elements of the theory of Lie groupoids and algebroids—definitions with examples, propositions and theorems—which constitute the conceptual core of the physically oriented considerations in the main text.

Definition B.1
.

A
groupoid
is a small category with all morphisms invertible. Thus, it is a septuple
{\rm{\bf Gr}}=({\rm Ob}{\rm{\bf Gr}}\equiv M,{\rm Mor}{\rm{\bf Gr}}\equiv\mathscr{G},s,t,{\rm Id},{\rm m}\equiv.,{\rm Inv}\equiv(\cdot)^{-1})
—to be abbreviated as
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
—which is composed of a pair of sets:

•

the
object set

M
;

•

the
arrow set

\mathscr{G}
,

and a quintuple of
structure maps
:

•

the
source
(
map
)
s\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to M
;

•

the
target
(
map
)
t\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to M
;

•

the
unit
(
map
)
{\rm Id}\hskip-2.0pt:M\to\mathscr{G},\ m\mapsto{\rm Id}_{m}
;

•

the
inverse
(
map
)
{\rm Inv}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to\mathscr{G},\ g\mapsto{\rm Inv}(g)\equiv g^{-1}
;

•

the
multiplication
(
map
)
{\rm m}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\hskip-2.0pt{}_{s}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{G}\to\mathscr{G},\ (g,h)\mapsto{\rm m}(g,h)\equiv g.h
,

subject to the conditions (in force whenever the expressions are well-defined):

(i)

s(g.h)=s(h),\ t(g.h)=t(g)
;

(ii)

(g.h).k=g.(h.k)
;

(iii)

{\rm Id}_{t(g)}.g=g=g.{\rm Id}_{s(g)}

;

(iv)

s(g^{-1})=t(g),\ t(g^{-1})=s(g),\ g.g^{-1}={\rm Id}_{t(g)},\ g^{-1}.g={\rm Id}_{s(g)}
.

A
morphism
between two groupoids
{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{A},\ A\in\{1,2\}
is a functor
\Phi\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{1}\to{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{2}
.

A
Lie groupoid
is a groupoid whose object and arrow sets are smooth manifolds, whose structure maps are smooth, and whose source and target maps are surjective submersions. A morphism between two Lie groupoids is a functor between them with smooth object and morphism components.

A Lie groupoid is called

•

transitive
if the
anchor

(t,s)\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to M\times M
is surjective;

•

locally trivial
if
(t,s)\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to M\times M
is a surjective submersion.

Example B.2
.

Every Lie group
({\rm G},{\rm m}_{\rm G},{\rm Inv}_{\rm G},e)
gives rise to a Lie groupoid

\displaystyle\mathbf{B}{\rm G}\equiv\bigl(\{\bullet\},{\rm G},\bullet,\bullet,e,{\rm m}_{\rm G},{\rm Inv}_{\rm G}\bigr)\,,

with the singleton
\{\bullet\}
as the object manifold. It is termed the
delooping
(
groupoid
) of
{\rm G}
.

Example B.3
.

Every manifold
M\in{\rm{\bf Man}}
gives rise to a Lie groupoid

\displaystyle{\rm Pair}(M)\equiv\bigl(M,M\times M,{\rm pr}_{2},{\rm pr}_{1},\Delta,{\rm pr}_{1,4},\tau\bigr)\,,

with unit
\Delta\hskip-2.0pt:M\to M\times M,\ m\mapsto(m,m)
, multiplication
{\rm pr}_{1,4}\hskip-2.0pt:(M\times M)\ \hskip-2.0pt{}_{{\rm pr}_{2}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{{\rm pr}_{1}}\hskip-2.0pt(M\times M)\to M\times M,\ ((m_{4},m_{2}),(m_{2},m_{1}))\mapsto(m_{4},m_{1})
, and inverse
\tau\hskip-2.0pt:M\times M\to M\times M,\ (m_{1},m_{2})\mapsto(m_{2},m_{1})
. It is called the
pair groupoid
of
M
.

Example B.4
.

Given
M,Y\in{\rm{\bf Man}}
and a surjective submersion
\pi\hskip-2.0pt:Y\twoheadrightarrow M
, there arises a Lie groupoid

\displaystyle{\rm Pair}_{\pi}(Y)\equiv\bigl(Y,Y\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\pi}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\pi}\hskip-2.0ptY,{\rm pr}_{2},{\rm pr}_{1},\Delta,{\rm pr}_{1,4},\tau\bigr)\subset{\rm Pair}(Y)\,,

defined in the notation of Ex.
B.3
. It is called the
submersion groupoid
of
\pi
.

Example B.5
.

Given a Lie group
{\rm G}
and a manifold
M
on which
{\rm G}
acts smoothly as
\lambda\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\to{\rm Diff}(M)
, there arises a Lie groupoid

\displaystyle{\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M\equiv\bigl(M,{\rm G}\times M,{\rm pr}_{2},\widetilde{\lambda}\equiv{\rm ev}\circ(\lambda\times{\rm id}_{M}),(e,\cdot),({\rm m}_{\rm G}\circ{\rm pr}_{1,3},{\rm pr}_{4}),({\rm Inv}_{\rm G}\circ{\rm pr}_{1},\widetilde{\lambda})\bigr)\,,

defined in terms of the evaluation map
{\rm ev}\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm Diff}(M)\times M\to M,\ (f,m)\mapsto f(m)
. It is called the
action groupoid
of
\lambda
. By a mild abuse of the notation, we identify
\lambda
and
\widetilde{\lambda}
in this work.

Example B.6
.

[
Wei87
,
CDW87
]

A Lie groupoid
(M,\mathscr{G},s,t,{\rm Id},{\rm m},{\rm Inv})
is termed
symplectic
if there exists a closed non-degenerate 2-form
\omega\in\Omega^{2}(\mathscr{G})
, which makes
(\mathscr{G},\omega)
a symplectic manifold, and such that the graph of
{\rm m}
is a lagrangean submanifold in
(\mathscr{G}^{\times 3},({\rm pr}_{1}^{*}+{\rm pr}_{2}^{*}-{\rm pr}_{3}^{*})\omega)
. As shown in
[
CDW87
, Thm. 1.1, Chap. II]
, the object manifold
M
then carries a canonical Poisson bivector
\Pi\in\Gamma(\bigwedge^{2}{\rm T}M)
, relative to which
s
is Poisson, and
t
is anti-Poisson. Furthermore,
{\rm Id}(M)
is lagrangean.

Definition B.7

(
[
MM03
]
)
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.1
. A (
global
)
bisection of

{\rm{\bf Gr}}
is a section
\beta\hskip-2.0pt:M\to\mathscr{G}
of the surjective submersion
s\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\to M
such that the induced map

\displaystyle t_{*}\beta\equiv t\circ\beta\hskip-2.0pt:M\longrightarrow M

is a diffeomorphism. Equivalently, it is a submanifold
S\subset\mathscr{G}
with the property that both restrictions:
s\big|_{S}
and
t\big|_{S}
are diffeomorphisms. We shall denote the set of bisections as

\displaystyle{\rm Bisec({\bf Gr})}\equiv{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\,.

A
local bisection of

{\rm{\bf Gr}}
is a local section
\beta\hskip-2.0pt:O\to\mathscr{G}
of
s
over an open subset
O\subset M
, such that the induced map

\displaystyle t_{*}\beta\equiv t\circ\beta\hskip-2.0pt:O\longrightarrow(t\circ\beta)(O)

is a diffeomorphism. We shall denote the set of local bisections as

\displaystyle{\rm Bisec}_{\rm loc}({\rm{\bf Gr}})\equiv{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})\,.

Definition B.8
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. The
group of bisections
of a Lie groupoid
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
is the canonical structure of a group on
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
. Its binary operation is defined as

\displaystyle\cdot\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\times{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G}),\ (\beta_{2},\beta_{1})\longmapsto\beta_{2}\bigl(t_{*}\beta_{1}(\cdot)\bigr).\beta_{1}(\cdot)\equiv\beta_{2}\cdot\beta_{1}\,.

The neutral element is
{\rm Id}
, also termed the
unit bisection
, and the corresponding inverse is

\displaystyle{\rm Inv}\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G}),\ \beta\longmapsto{\rm Inv}\circ\beta\circ\bigl(t_{*}\beta\bigr)^{-1}\equiv\beta^{-1}\,.

Similarly, the
group of local bisections
of
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
is the canonical structure of a group on
{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})
. Its binary operation is defined as

\displaystyle\cdot\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})\times{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G}),\ (\beta_{2},\beta_{1})\longmapsto\beta_{2}\bigl(t_{*}\beta_{1}(\cdot)\bigr).\beta_{1}(\cdot)\big|_{(t_{*}\beta_{1})^{-1}({\rm dom}(\beta_{2}))\cap{\rm dom}(\beta_{1})}\equiv\beta_{2}\cdot\beta_{1}\,.

The neutral element is
{\rm Id}
, and the corresponding inverse is

\displaystyle{\rm Inv}\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G}),\ \beta\longmapsto{\rm Inv}\circ\beta\circ\bigl(t_{*}\beta\bigr)^{-1}\big|_{t_{*}\beta({\rm dom}(\beta))}\equiv\beta^{-1}\,.

Example B.9
.

Adopt the notation of Ex.
B.2
. There exists a canonical isomorphism
{\rm Bisec}(\mathbf{B}{\rm G})\cong{\rm G}
.

Example B.10
.

Adopt the notation of Ex.
B.3
. There exists a canonical isomorphism
{\rm Bisec}({\rm Pair}(M))\cong{\rm Diff}(M)
.

Example B.11
.

Adopt the notation of Ex.
B.5
. The group
{\rm Bisec}({\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M)
contains a subgroup

\displaystyle{\rm G}\cong\iota({\rm G})\subset{\rm Bisec}({\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M)\,,

given by the image of the monomorphism

\displaystyle\iota\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm G}\longrightarrow{\rm Bisec}({\rm G}\,{\hskip-1.13791pt\ltimes\hskip-1.42271pt}_{\lambda}M),\ g\longmapsto(g,\cdot)\,.

We shall refer to bisections in that image as
flat
.

Example B.12
.

[
CDW87
,
Ryb01
]

For the symplectic groupoid from Ex.
B.6
, the group
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
contains a subgroup

(B.2)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G},\omega)

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\bigl\{\ \beta\in{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\quad|\quad\beta(M)\subset\mathscr{G}\textrm{ is lagrangean}\ \bigr\}

\displaystyle\equiv

\displaystyle\bigl\{\ \beta\in{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\quad|\quad\beta^{*}\omega=0\ \bigr\}\subset{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\,.

These bisections are called
lagrangean
, and the subgroup
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G},\omega)
shall be referred to as the
lagrangean group
of
\mathscr{G}
.

Definition B.13
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. A Lie groupoid
\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 6.92361pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-6.92361pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 21.14998pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt
with the property:

\displaystyle\forall\ g\in\mathscr{G}\ \exists\ \beta\in{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\hskip-2.0pt:\beta\bigl(s(g)\bigr)=g

shall be termed
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
-complete
.

Example B.14
.

All source- resp. target-connected Lie groupoids are
{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
-complete (see:
[
ZL09
, Thm. 3.1]
), and so is also every action groupoid from Ex.
B.5
.

Proposition/Definition B.15
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. Every bisection
\beta\in{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})
determines, over each point
m\in{\rm dom}(\beta)
, a direct-sum decomposition

\displaystyle{\rm T}_{\beta(m)}\mathscr{G}\cong{\rm T}_{\beta(m)}\bigl(\beta({\rm dom}(\beta))\bigr)\oplus\bigl({\rm ker}\,{\rm T}s\bigr)_{\beta(m)}\,.

We shall call the corresponding pair
(\chi_{\beta},\upsilon_{\beta})
of complementary projectors,

\displaystyle\chi_{\beta}(m)={\rm T}_{\beta(m)}(\beta\circ s)\,,\qquad\qquad\upsilon_{\beta}(m)={\rm id}_{{\rm T}_{\beta(m)}\mathscr{G}}-\chi_{\beta}(m)\,,

the
splitting
of
{\rm T}\mathscr{G}\big|_{\beta({\rm dom}(\beta))}

induced by

\beta
.

Definition B.16
.

[
CS15
, Sec. 3.1]

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. The
first-jet groupoid
of
\mathscr{G}
is the groupoid

\displaystyle\bigl(M,J^{1}\mathscr{G},\pi_{J^{1}},\tau,j^{1}{\rm Id},j^{1}{\rm m},j^{1}{\rm Inv}\bigr)

with the arrow manifold
J^{1}\mathscr{G}
consisting of first jets
j^{1}_{m}\beta
of local bisections
\beta\in{\mathbb{B}}_{\rm loc}(\mathscr{G})
(
{\rm dom}(\beta)\ni m
) over
M
, and with source
\pi_{J^{1}}(j^{1}_{m}\beta)=m
and target
\tau(j^{1}_{m}\beta)=t_{*}\beta(m)
, identity
j^{1}{\rm Id}(m)=j^{1}_{m}{\rm Id}
, multiplication
j^{1}{\rm m}(j^{1}_{t_{*}\beta_{1}(m)}\beta_{2},j^{1}_{m}\beta_{1})=j^{1}_{m}(\beta_{2}\cdot\beta_{1})
, and inverse
j^{1}{\rm Inv}(j^{1}_{m}\beta)=j^{1}_{t_{*}\beta(m)}(\beta^{-1})
.

Proposition B.17
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.16
. There exists a group homomorphism

(B.3)

\displaystyle j^{1}\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}(J^{1}\mathscr{G}),\ \beta\longmapsto j^{1}_{\cdot}\beta\,.

Definition B.18
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. The
shadow action of

{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})

on

M
is

\displaystyle t_{*}\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\times M\longrightarrow M,\ (\beta,m)\longmapsto t\bigl(\beta(m)\bigr)\,.

We refer by the same name to and use the same symbol for the group homomorphism

(B.4)

\displaystyle t_{*}\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow{\rm Diff}(M)\,.

Definition B.19
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.7
. The
left-multiplication of

\mathscr{G}

by

{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
is the left action

\displaystyle L\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\times\mathscr{G}\longrightarrow\mathscr{G},\ \bigl(\beta,g\bigr)\longmapsto\beta\bigl(t\bigl(g\bigr)\bigr).g\equiv L_{\beta}\bigl(g\bigr)\equiv\beta\vartriangleright g\,.

The
right-multiplication of

\mathscr{G}

by

{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
is the right action

\displaystyle R\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\times{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\longrightarrow\mathscr{G},\ \bigl(g,\beta\bigr)\longmapsto g.\bigl(\beta^{-1}\bigl(s\bigl(g\bigr)\bigr)\bigr)^{-1}\equiv R{}_{\beta}\bigl(g\bigr)\equiv g\vartriangleleft\beta\,.

The
conjugation of

\mathscr{G}

by

{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})
is the
left
action

\displaystyle C\hskip-2.0pt:{\mathbb{B}}(\mathscr{G})\times\mathscr{G}\longrightarrow\mathscr{G},\ (\beta,g)\longmapsto\beta\bigl(t(g)\bigr).g.\beta\bigl(s(g)\bigr)^{-1}\equiv C_{\beta}(g)\equiv\beta\vartriangleright g\vartriangleleft\beta^{-1}\,.

Definition B.20
.

Adopt the notation of Def.
B.1
. A
right-
\mathscr{G}
-module space
, or a
right-
\mathscr{G}
-module
for short, is a triple
(X,\mu,\varrho)
composed of

•

a smooth manifold
X
;

•

a smooth map
\mu\hskip-2.0pt:X\to M
, called the (
right
)
moment map
;

•

a smooth map

\displaystyle\varrho\hskip-2.0pt:X\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{G}\longrightarrow X,\ (x,g)\longmapsto\varrho(x,g)\equiv\varrho_{g}(x)\equiv x\blacktriangleleft g\,,

termed the (
right
)
action
(
map
),

subject to the relations (in force whenever the expressions are well-defined):

(GrM1)

\mu(x\blacktriangleleft g)=s(g)
;

(GrM2)

x\blacktriangleleft{\rm Id}_{\mu(x)}=x
;

(GrM3)

(x\blacktriangleleft g)\blacktriangleleft h=x\blacktriangleleft(g.h)
.

Similarly, a
left-
\mathscr{G}
-module
(
space
) is a triple
(X,\mu,\lambda)
composed of

•

a smooth manifold
X
;

•

a smooth map
\mu\hskip-2.0pt:X\to M
, called the (
left
)
moment map
;

•

a smooth map

\displaystyle\lambda\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{s}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\mu}\hskip-2.0ptX\longrightarrow X,\ (g,x)\longmapsto\lambda(g,x)\equiv\lambda_{g}(x)\equiv g\blacktriangleright x\,,

termed the (
left
)
action
(
map
),

subject to the relations (in force whenever the expressions are well-defined):

(GlM1)

\mu(g\blacktriangleright x)=t(g)
;

(GlM2)

{\rm Id}_{\mu(x)}\blacktriangleright x=x
;

(GlM3)

h\blacktriangleright(g\blacktriangleright x)=(h.g)\blacktriangleright x
.

A right action
\varrho
is termed
free
if the following implication obtains:

\displaystyle x\blacktriangleleft g=x\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g={\rm Id}_{\mu(x)}\,,

so that, in particular, the
isotropy group

\mathscr{G}_{m}=s^{-1}(\{m\})\cap t^{-1}(\{m\})
of
m\in M
acts freely (in the usual sense) on the fibre
\mu^{-1}(\{m\})
. A free left action is defined analogously.

A right action
\varrho
is termed
transitive
if for any two points
x,x^{\prime}\in X
there exists an arrow
g\in\mathscr{G}
such that
x^{\prime}=x\blacktriangleleft g
. A transitive left action is defined analogously.

The subset

\displaystyle\mathscr{G}\blacktriangleright x:=\bigl\{\ g\blacktriangleright x\quad|\quad g\in s^{-1}\bigl(\mu(x)\bigr)\ \bigr\}

is called the
left
\mathscr{G}
-orbit
of
x\in X
.
Right
\mathscr{G}
-orbits
are defined analogously.

Let
{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{a}\equiv\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 9.34244pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-9.34244pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}_{a}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M_{a}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\ a\in\{1,2\}
be a pair of Lie groupoids, and let
(X_{a},\mu_{a},\varrho_{a})
be the respective
right-
\mathscr{G}_{a}
-modules. A
morphism
between the latter is a pair
(\Theta,\Phi)
consisting of a smooth manifold map

together with a functor
\Phi\hskip-2.0pt:{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{1}\to{\rm{\bf Gr}}_{2}
for which the following diagrams commute

\hskip-5.0pt\begin{aligned} \lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 9.34244pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-9.34244pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}_{a}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise-1.07639pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 23.5688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{M_{a}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{aligned}\hskip-3.0pt,\ a\in\{1,2\}
be Lie groupoids. A
(\mathscr{G}_{1},\mathscr{G}_{2})
-bibundle
is a quintuple
(\widehat{P};\mu_{1},\lambda_{1};\mu_{2},\varrho_{2})
composed of

•

a smooth manifold
\widehat{P}
, termed the
total space
;

•

smooth maps
\mu_{a}\hskip-2.0pt:\widehat{P}\to M_{a},\ a\in\{1,2\}
, termed the
left
(
a=1
) and
right
(
a=2
)
moment map
, respectively;

•

a smooth map
\lambda_{1}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathscr{G}_{1}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{s_{1}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\mu_{1}}\hskip-2.0pt\widehat{P}\to\widehat{P}
, termed the
left action
, and

•

a smooth map
\varrho_{2}\hskip-2.0pt:\widehat{P}\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu_{2}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t_{2}}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{G}_{2}\to\widehat{P}
, termed the
right action
,

such that

•

(\widehat{P},\mu_{1},\lambda_{1}\equiv\blacktriangleright)
is a left
\mathscr{G}_{1}
-module;

•

(\widehat{P},\mu_{2},\varrho_{2}\equiv\blacktriangleleft)
is a right
\mathscr{G}_{2}
-module;

•

the two actions commute with one another, i.e., we have, for all
(g_{1},p,g_{2})\in\mathscr{G}_{1}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{s_{1}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\mu_{1}}\hskip-2.0pt\widehat{P}\hskip-2.0pt{}_{\mu_{2}}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{t_{2}}\hskip-2.0pt\mathscr{G}_{2}
, the identity
(g_{1}\blacktriangleright p)\blacktriangleleft g_{2}=g_{1}\blacktriangleright(p\blacktriangleleft g_{2})
;

•

each moment map is invariant with respect to the other action, i.e., we have the identities
\mu_{1}(p\blacktriangleleft g_{2})=\mu_{1}(p)
and
\mu_{2}(g_{1}\blacktriangleright p)=\mu_{2}(p)
.

Whenever
(\widehat{P},M_{2},\mu_{2},\mu_{1},\lambda_{1})
is a (left) principal
\mathscr{G}_{1}
-bundle (with base

(\widehat{P},M_{1},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\varrho_{2})

\mathscr{G}_{2}
-bundle (with base

B.28
, we call
(\widehat{P};\mu_{1},\lambda_{1};\mu_{2},\varrho_{2})
a (
bi
)
principal
(\mathscr{G}_{1},\mathscr{G}_{2})
-bibundle

Definition B.33
.

Let
X
be a smooth manifold. A (
real
)
Lie algebroid over

X
(
of rank

N\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\times}
) is a triple
((\mathcal{E},X,{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\pi_{\mathcal{E}}),\alpha_{\mathcal{E}},[\cdot,\cdot]_{\mathcal{E}})
composed of

•

a vector bundle
(\mathcal{E},X,{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\pi_{\mathcal{E}})
, with total space
\mathscr{E}
, base
X
, typical fibre
{\mathbb{R}}^{N}
, and base projection
\pi_{\mathcal{E}}\hskip-2.0pt:\mathcal{E}\to X
;

•

a (vertical) vector-bundle morphism

(X,\mu,\lambda)
).

Proof.

The statement of the theorem follows straightforwardly from the following observation:

\displaystyle(V,v)\in{\rm T}_{(g,x)}\bigl(\mathscr{G}\,\hskip-2.0pt{}_{s}\hskip-3.0pt\times_{\mu}\hskip-2.0ptX\bigr)\subset{\rm T}_{g}\mathscr{G}\oplus{\rm T}_{x}X\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad{\rm T}_{g}s(V)={\rm T}_{x}\mu(v)\,,

put in conjunction with
({\rm ker}\,{\rm T}\widetilde{s})_{(g,x)}\equiv{\rm ker}\,{\rm T}_{(g,x)}{\rm pr}_{2}\equiv({\rm ker}\,{\rm T}s)_{g}\subset{\rm T}_{g}\mathscr{G}\subset{\rm T}_{g}\mathscr{G}\oplus{\rm T}_{x}X
, and so also
(\widetilde{\rm Id}^{*}{\rm ker}\,{\rm T}\widetilde{s})_{x}\equiv({\rm ker}\,{\rm T}\widetilde{s})_{({\rm Id}_{\mu(x)},x)}\equiv({\rm ker}\,{\rm T}s)_{{\rm Id}_{\mu(x)}}\equiv\mathscr{E}_{\mu(x)}
, and subsequently combined with the identification
{\rm T}\widetilde{t}\equiv{\rm T}\lambda
.
∎

Appendix C
Simplicial tools, and the Bott–Schulman–Stasheff cohomology

Below, we list the requisites of the simplicial model of equivariant cohomology of Lie groupoids and its sheaf-theoretic resolution employed in the discussion of multiplicative BSS extensions of de Rham cohomology classes and their geometrisations.

Convention C.1
.

Let
\triangle
be the standard simplex category, with objects
[n]=\{0,1,2,\ldots,n\}\subset{\mathbb{N}}
(see, e.g.:
[
Kan57
]
). We denote the standard generators of its
\hom
-sets (of order-preserving maps) as

\displaystyle\delta^{(n+1)}_{i}\hskip-2.0pt:[n]\longrightarrow[n+1],\ k\longmapsto\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}k&{\rm if}\ k<i\\
k+1&{\rm if}\ k\geq i\end{array}\right.\,,\qquad i\in\overline{0,n}

(
coface maps
), and

\displaystyle\sigma^{(n)}_{j}\hskip-2.0pt:[n+1]\longrightarrow[n],\ k\longmapsto\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}k&{\rm if}\ k\leq j\\
k-1&{\rm if}\ k>j\end{array}\right.\,,\qquad j\in\overline{0,n}

(
codegeneracy maps
).

Definition C.2
.

For
n\in{\mathbb{N}}
, the
topological
n
-simplex
is the topological space

\displaystyle\triangle^{n}:=\bigl\{\ (t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n+1})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{\times n+1}\quad|\quad\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\,t_{k}=1\ \bigr\}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{\times n+1}\,.

For
i\in\overline{0,n+1}
, the
i^{\rm th}

n
-face inclusion
is the map

\displaystyle\partial_{i}^{(n+1)}\hskip-2.0pt:\triangle^{n}\longrightarrow\triangle^{n+1},\ (t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n+1})\longmapsto(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{i},0,t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\ldots,t_{n+1})\,.

Definition C.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. A
simplicial object
in
\mathcal{C}
is a presheaf
C_{\bullet}\hskip-2.0pt:\triangle^{\rm op}\to\mathcal{C}
. The functorial images of the generators of the
\hom
-sets
\triangle([k],[l]),\ k,l\in{\mathbb{N}}
are called
face maps

d^{(n+1)}_{i}=C_{\bullet}(\delta^{(n+1)}_{i}),\ i\in\overline{0,n}
and
degeneracy maps

s^{(n)}_{j}=C_{\bullet}(\sigma^{(n)}_{j}),\ j\in\overline{0,n}
(defined for all
n\in{\mathbb{N}}
), respectively. Given simplicial objects
C^{a}_{\bullet},\ a\in\{1,2\}
, a
simplicial morphism
between them is a natural transformation
\eta\hskip-2.0pt:C^{1}_{\bullet}\Rightarrow C^{2}_{\bullet}
.

In particular, a simplicial object
M_{\bullet}\hskip-2.0pt:\triangle^{\rm op}\to{\rm{\bf Man}}
in the category
{\rm{\bf Man}}
of smooth manifolds is termed a
simplicial manifold
. Its (smooth) face maps determine the
Dupont operators

\displaystyle\Delta^{(\bullet)}_{(n)}:=\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}\,(-1)^{k}\,d_{k}^{(n+1)*}\hskip-2.0pt:\Omega^{\bullet}(M_{n})\longrightarrow\Omega^{\bullet}(M_{n+1})

on differential forms on its component objects
M_{n}=M_{\bullet}([n])\in{\rm{\bf Man}}
.

.

]

Example C.5
.

Let
M\in{\rm{\bf Man}}
, and let
\mathcal{O}=\{O_{i}\}_{i\in I}
be an open cover of
M
. The manifold
\check{Y}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\bigsqcup_{i\in I}\,O_{i}
(endowed with the standard disjoint-sum topology and smooth structure inherited from the submanifolds
